speechtext:
We will have it within another year, when the hydro-electric power commission will turn into the wires an additional million and a half horsepower from the gigantic dams being built up the Ottawa river. In addition, in two years time we will have available the big power plant to be constructed at Windsor. Therefore if we do not have the power now we soon will have it. The hydroelectric power commission is a concrete example of the result of the production of a vast number of kilowatt hours of cheap electricity distributed throughout the province of Ontario. No one knows better than the Ontario hydro-electric power commission that the expansion in this province has resulted from an abundance of cheap electricity; and this is also well understood in Quebec.
I believe I had come to the suggested new power plant for Cape Breton island. I should like to see another 25,000 horsepower plant in the New Glasgow-Westville-Stellarton area. They are almost up to capacity now, and one big new plant would meet their additional needs at the moment and leave a surplus for 5849-276J
expansion. I also believe both the Minto area and the Saint John area in New Brunswick should have new power plants of not less than
25,000	horsepower capacity. There should be a new plant at Moncton, another at Bathurst, perhaps one at Campbellton in the north, and one down in the southwestern portion of New Brunswick. While I am at it, I believe I left out the southwestern portion of Nova Scotia, which generation after generation, has been more or less standing still, largely because of lack of power. A plant should be erected there. As Nova Scotia has the coal; why should it not have the power?
Now I come back to Prince Edward Island. I mentioned the power plant at Charlottetown. There is another small plant at Summerside with a capacity of about 1,500 kilowatt hours. A plant of 25,000 horsepower capacity at Charlottetown would permit the distribution of power throughout the island, and I am sure production would expand like nobody's business. I have been from one end of the Mand to the other. The power situation at Charlottetown is fairly good at the moment, but there is not much for the rest of the island. They must be given a chance to expand and develop their own resources, to produce in their home plants; and nothing will bring about that result better than an abundance of cheap electricity. I urge as strongly as possible, that these suggestions be adopted, because I am convinced that only by some such program can the maritime provinces expand. Their primary and secondary industries can be greatly enlarged, and that is essential if they are to expand economically so that their people may have something to do at home.
You may ask how all this has come about. Well, everywhere I went I asked engineers, "What would you recommend that the federal government do?" and I am going to tell you what these engineers suggested. Probably there will be other suggestions, some perhaps better than these; but the first one given me was that the federal government should advance one-third of the cost of that power program in the maritimes and one-third of the cost of rural electrification. That is what we did here in Ontario. We paid one-third of the cost for protection against floods on the Grand river, which amounted to a large sum of money. It is a suggestion which might be worth considering. In the case of the maritimes, the government could do what they are doing in the western provinces. I shall refer to that in another debate.
Next, they could make an outright capital grant as is done in western Canada in connection with conservation of water and re-
434;
The Budget-Mr. MacNicol

clamation programs. In western Canada outright capital grants are made under P.F.R.A. for the building of dams and dug-outs, and the same thing could be done in the maritimes.
Next, the federal government could lend money to build new power plants or to modernize or make additions to present large plants, including interlocking provincial grid transmission systems, at a rate of two per cent, repayable in forty years. Which one of these plans would be the most attractive to maritimers, I do not know.
Next, pay a subsidy of one mill per kilowatt hour for ten years for power produced and sold, or its equivalent, $1.25 a ton on maritime coal used in the production of electricity and its distribution throughout the maritime provinces.
There is a program that will bring results. I do not look upon it as being a mere matter of cost, because the federal government would reap a return in the form of sales and income taxes, and after a while in the form of succession duties, a hundred times more than what they would put into it. Aside from that, it is imperative that we do something to assist the maritime provinces. The Canadian Press dispatch which I quoted earlier refers to the average income in the maritimes as compared with elsewhere. Stop to think what it would mean if we could bring the average income in the maritimes up to the average income in Ontario.
I do not want anyone to think that in talking about the maritimes I am not talking for Davenport riding, Ontario. If such a program were carried out, Davenport riding, which I have the honour to represent, and Toronto and Ontario and Quebec would profit. As I said a few moments ago, one of the immediate results of the new power plant at Maccan was the building of a new salt plant at Amherst. This is a very fine plant employing 100 or perhaps more men and women. It is well worth going to see.
When I went through it I examined the machinery to see where it came from. I found that some of the machinery came from the fine city of Brantford. I found that the radiators were from the plant in Toronto in which I worked for many years. The evaporators had had been made in Owen Sound, in the riding of the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Case). Other machinery had been made in Hamilton, and much of the electrical equipment came from Sherbrooke, Quebec. This shows that that new salt plant brought business to Ontario and Quebec.

I do not know of any better way by which I can help my riding. I never talk about my riding, because I want to see the country opened up. I know that, as the country is opened up, the factories in my riding will get something to do. Just recently an announcement was made that another new plant is to be erected in Amherst by the Bendix Corporation at a cost of S9,000,000, to employ 750 people. I say without fear of successful contradiction that if cheap power is made available in the maritimes, along with proper means of transmission throughout the length and breadth of the provinces, those provinces will expand as they have not expanded since confederation.
If anyone else can tell me of any other plan that will put the maritime provinces on their feet I should like to hear it. I know that Ontario and Quebec have expanded greatly because of their cheap power. I spend my time in travelling and I try to do what I can to help Canada. I know that as the west expands, as the maritimes expand, they will order materials from Ontario and Quebec. We will get our part of it. We should all go along together. One part of the country cannot be prosperous with other parts not prosperous.
I have done my best on this occasion to present a program which, on the basis of many years of travel and survey in England, the United States and Canada I am convinced will bring about the economic rebuilding of the maritime provinces on a scale never dreamed possible.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to compliment the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) upon his excellent talk on the maritimes. Sometimes Toronto is accused of being selfish, but we can never accuse the hon. member for Davenport of that. He is always thinking of other parts of the country, for which attitude he is to be complimented.
Many hon. members who have spoken in this debate have prefaced their remarks by saying that the budget is a disappointment.
I do not think it is a disappointment; I think it is exactly the type of budget we could expect to get from our present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I do not think the people of Canada expected to get water out of a stone, and they did not get it in this budget.
However, the Minister of Finance must be realistic. I think it is time that we had realistic people as ministers of finance in this country. The minister is reported on page 4063 of Hansard as saying:
I believe that all parties in this parliament and most Canadians share the view that the

The Budget-Mr. Wright
national budget is no longer merely a matter of the government accounts that should be balanced every twelve months on some financial rule of thumb. We view the national budget now as an integral part of the nation's business, influenced by and having an influence upon the state of employment, income and prices.
Again he states:
This government and this parliament must accept a considerable measure of responsibility for influencing and, indeed, directing economic trends in so far as that can be done within the framework of our political and economic principles. Were we only a small municipality, unable to influence the mighty economic forces determining the prosperity of our citizens, it would still be wise for us to look further ahead than this year and to put something by at present.
I think that is a realistic point of view_ to take. In the past we have been like the ostrich, burying our heads in the sand and trying to make out that budgets did not affect our everyday life. However, today we recognize the fact and face up to the responsibility that budgets have a real influence and that they can be used to balance our economy and maintain a proper relationship between consumption and production in our country. Our hon. friends to the right in the Conservative party say that this is too great a power to be given to the government. However I think it is only the people's representatives who should and must accept that responsibility.
In my opinion the minister was wise in budgeting for a surplus at this time, although I do not agree that that surplus should have been the amount that it was, some $670 million. I think this year and next year the minister would be justified in budgeting for a surplus of probably $500 million. The minister should be straightforward in the matter. He should have given to parliament last year a more correct estimate of what our surplus would be.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: He did the best he could.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It seems to me that there was too great a difference between the estimate of $190 million and the $670 million which we attained. This year we budgeted for a surplus of some $489 million. We hope that is more nearly correct than last year's estimate, and it probably will be.
Surpluses are not something that we should be ashamed of. As businessmen or farmers we are rather proud if we get a surplus. That is what we are working for, and government surpluses should be viewed in somewhat the same light. But there is a difference between a government surplus and a surplus which the average individual or business attains through individual effort. The government gets it surplus through the efforts of the Canadian people as a whole, from their industry and from the taxes which the government collects from them as a result of that industry. It is not the surplus that matters so much as how you attain the surplus and from whom you get it, and I am afraid that is where the minister and I shall have to part company, because I cannot agree with him in some of the methods by which he has accumulated his present surplus.
I think we have come to agree in Canada that direct taxation is fairer than indirect taxation. People should know where the taxes are coming from. In 1946-47 the minister collected by direct taxation $1,412,156,000, and in 1947-48 the estimate was $1,286,878,000, or a decrease of some $125,278,000. On the other hand in indirect taxes, in 1946-47 the minister collected $1,022,129,000, and in 1947-48 $1,134,325,000, or an increase of $112,196,000.
The minister would have been better advised had he collected more in direct taxes and less in indirect taxes, because direct taxation is a fairer means of taxation. But the situation is even more disturbing when we analyse the figures to determine just which direct taxes are being increased and which are being decreased.
In the personal income tax field, for instance, the minister collected in 1946-47, $694,530,000 and in 1947-48, $659,828,000, or a decrease of roughly $40,000,000. On the other hand, in 1946-47 he collected, through the excess profits tax, $448,698,000, while in 1947-48 he collected only $227,000,000. The excess profits tax was discontinued as of the first of January of this year. The excess profits tax has yielded a lot of money to the tax funds of this government during past years; in round figures, it yielded in 1943-44, $468 million; 1944-45, $465 million; 1945-46, $494 million; 1946-47, $448 million.
The minister in his budget-and the other members of the government have so stated- said that it was necessary to remove this tax to encourage production in this country, that when we wanted to increase production we had to give some incentive to industry to expand in order to obtain that increased production. If it is necessary to give industry an added incentive to produce, I think it is also necessary to give the farmer's of this country some added incentive for increased production, and to give the worker in the factory some added incentive to put in a little more overtime to increase production. But the minister has not given the same incentive to these primary producers as he has given to industry by the removal of the excess profits tax.
The Budget-Mr. Wright

If he had raised the income tax exemptions for the lower income groups to SI,250 for a single person and S2,500 for a married person we would have got a great deal more production. I know there is no single factor in the agricultural areas of Canada that has held up production to a greater extent than the income tax. Whether we like it or not, the farmers, as hon. members who have contacts with our agricultural areas well know, are saying that they are not going to milk cows to pay income tax, and that they are not going to feed pigs to pay income tax. Unless some incentive is given to the primary producers in this country to increase production, we can expect a rising cost of living because of the scarcity of essential food products. The Minister of Finance might very well have considered giving some exemptions to the primary producers engaged in the production of foodstuffs and to the working men who are employed in the factories and producing all our goods and services.
In my opinion the government is itself to blame for inflation in this country: first, by removing controls; second, by removing the excess profits tax, and at the same time encouraging the reinvestment of millions of dollars which might have been paid in taxation, in expenditure on new plant and equipment by allowing double depreciation on new and reconverted plants and equipment. The minister admitted in his budget speech that it is this capital expansion which is taking place in Canada that worries him, and yet the government deliberately set out to encourage this capital expansion. I have in my hand a government pamphlet entitled "Encouragement to Industrial Expansion in Canada- Operation of Special Depreciation Provisions -November 10, 1944-March 31, 1949." It is published by the authority of the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Reconstruction and Supply. It is an enlightening pamphlet and gives the government's reasons for allowing special depreciation. It says at page 22:
The significance of this income tax deduction, frequently called "double depreciation," was that it permitted companies, while profits and taxes were high, to postpone the taxation on a portion of their profits to a later period when it was understood that taxes would be lower. The purpose of this provision was amplified by the Minister of Finance on June 26, 1944. in his budget speech: "First, it will allow the taxpayer to recover a part of his capital whenever earnings are good but will still leave all the income or profit actually realized from the venture over its whole life subject to taxation; second, it will allow him, in respect of such new investment carried out at a time when the government has declared the conversion and expansion of industry to be desirable, to transfer some of his income from a period when war-

time tax rates may still be in effect to a later period when he may expect normal taxation to be lower. To this extent, it will relieve such investment for postwar purposes from such wartime taxation of business profits as may still be in effect at the time the work of conversion or expansion is carried out.
The minister goes on to give certain examples of just what this will mean to the taxpayer who is expanding his plant and equipment. He said:
To take three companies each having an income before depreciation of $100,000 in 1945 and each having established standard profits of $50,000:	The first company having no investment in a new capital project -would pay a gross tax (income and excess profits tax) of $65,000, including a refundable tax portion of $8,333, or a net tax of $56,667. The second company making an investment of $250,000, of which $100,000- was for a building and $150,000 for machinery and equipment, would pay, after allowance of normal depreciation rates on new investment, a gross tax of $4-5.000 or a net tax of $40,667, after deducting the refundable tax portion of $4,333. The third company making the same investment expenditures and being permitted to charge double depreciation would pay -a gross tax of $25,00-0, including a refundable tax portion of $333 or a net tax of $24,667. The third company would thus be paying $1-6,000 less in taxes than the second company, and $32,0-0-0 less than the first. These amounts do not reflect the full savings by the investing companies using varying depreciation rates because some of the pro-fits, the distribution of which may be postponed, will be subject to taxation at a later date.
This provision really meant something to these companies, and as a result of that we find that the companies themselves have taken advantage of the provision to the extent that in 1945 they made application for and were granted $232 million in depreciation for the period of operation, November 10, 1944, to March 31. 1949; in 1946, $377 million, and in 1947, $845 million, or a total of $1,392 million, after cancellations, reinstatements and adjustments had been made. The house will notice that there is a very large increase during 1947. Naturally those companies which had excess profits in 1947, and which in the normal course of events -might have had to pay 85 per cent of these excess profits in -taxes, were anxious to expand their plant and equipment. because they knew the government had already announced that the excess profits tax was coming off at the end of 1947, and if they could keep that money out of the hands of the government for one year they knew they would be safe. Therefore naturally there was a tremendous increase in applications for double depreciation on plant and equipment during 1947. I say to the minister that was one of the main reasons for the rise in the

The Budget-Mr. Jackman
cost of living and the scarcity of materials that we had in Canada in 1947, and that we have in 1948.
The minister did not give the same concessions to the house builder; he did not give the same concessions to the farmer who wanted to buy land or to expand his plant as he gave to these companies in the class which I have just indicated. Let me give a little further analysis and show the size of the companies which received this special depreciation. On page 45 of this booklet the following appears:
Smaller projects involving expenditures of less than $100,000 were most numerous. They made up 77 per cent of all applications received, but involved' only $105 million or 8 per cent of total expenditures approved. On the other hand, 3 per cent of all applications were for projects of $1,000,000 and over, and comprised $815 million or 58 per cent of all investment expenditures contemplated. These figures indicate that the major part of the industrial investment program is due to the expansion of a small selected group of large industries.
It may be all right. I believe expansion is necessary in Canada, but I do not think the larger units, which quite possibly could have financed their own expansion, should have been given these special privileges with regard to depreciation. The same thing applies to the regions benefited. On page 9 of the booklet the following appears:
Ontario anticipates the largest amount of investment projects with approved special depreciation,. $605 million. Quebec is next in line with $509 million, followed by British Columbia with $165 million, the maritime region with $65 million, and the prairie region with $48 million.
Again the whole program has been one of centralization, centralization not only in regions but in the hands of small groups of tremendously large industries, which they have been able to build through special depreciation allowed by the government. That is where I disagree with the minister. I disagree with him in the method by which we attain these surpluses, and in the method of taxation that we are using in this country. It is time we recognized that small business has a place in Canada; that small business is the backbone, and must be the backbone, of our economy. Until we give it an equal opportunity with large industry, through the taxation policy that we follow in this country, then I am afraid that small industry cannot develop, nor can we spread our industries into the areas about which the hon. member for Davenport has just spoken. We should be able to distribute our industry more in Canada than is being done at the present time. It
is my opinion that the government, through its fiscal policy, can have an influence in the distribution of industry.
The government needs to adopt some new method of giving encouragement to production and the ownership of houses. If the government wishes to do that it might very well give consideration to an exemption of up to $1,000 on capital invested in a house or in a farm in this country. Thousands of our young men have come back from overseas and have settled on farms, some through the Veterans' Land Act and some on their own. Because of our present system of taxation, it will be almost impossible for these young fellows to pay for their farms. It is almost impossible for the average workingman to pay for a house because of the high cost of construction today, and that high cost is the result of the government's policy. One of the reasons for it is the government's policy of special depreciation, whereby large industries are going out and bidding for every bit of the available material in this country to use in the expansion of their own industries in order to take advantage of this special depreciation.
Let us be fair; let us give to all groups in this country an equal chance. That is my main criticism of the budget. I think the budget should be used as an instrument of fiscal policy, an instrument to give to all the people of Canada an equal opportunity.
Mr. HARRY R. JACKMAN (Rosedale): Mr. Speaker, in the two budgets which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has brought down he has been very fond of making records. In his first budget he brought down a surplus the like of which we had not seen in Canada. The budget which he brought down last Tuesday was the most disappointing budget in our history.
My colleague the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon), when he was home over the week end, was hailed by one of his constituents who asked whether the hon. member might put questions on the floor of the house. When my hon. friend replied "Yes", his constituent said, "Will you ask the Minister of Finance when the budget will be brought down?" Another man, one of my own constituents, said that this budget which we saw last week reminded him very much of the paraphrased quotation, "Abandon hope all ye who live and labour here."
During the war years the Canadian people were willing to stand any financial strain that might be put upon them and accounted it but a small sacrifice. But I do not suppose that any people in any other country during the war years had suffered such a tremendously
The Budget-Mr. Jackman

accelerated rate of taxation as did the Canadian people. From 1939 to 1944 our taxes rose from $500 million to over five times that amount; and now, with the federal government taking twenty-three cents out of every dollar of the people's earnings, the great question which this budget poses is this: Is Canada, by a silent revolution, rapidly becoming a bureaucrat-controlled state, or is individual freedom to survive? Revolutions can be silent as well as violent.
The second question is whether this is a production budget, or whether the high rate of taxation is destroying incentive, thus feeding the fires of inflation and taking bread out of the mouths of our people.
Contrary to the impression which the minister wished to give, taxation has decreased by an insignificant amount in total, and the rate of taxation is also very little reduced. The total amount to be taken in federal taxes, $2,384 million, is now almost as great as was the national income in 1933, when it amounted to $2,632 million. It is an amazing situation, to think the federal government is now taxing as much as the total national income was in 1933, and it is particularly amazing when we remember that the government creates nothing. The present budget offers no relief whatsoever in the personal income tax bracket, and it represents a reduction of only three per cent in total taxation from last year s extraordinary burden, when an unexpected surplus of $670 million was realized, or an amount equal to $55 per head for every man. woman and child.
Notwithstanding this unexpected windfall, the government refuses to reduce taxation. Surely the government is on the defensive, for there is not a taxpayer in the country who believes that its policy is either fair or sound.
_ Last year the Minister of Finance, with immodest pride, boasted that he had produced not only the largest surplus but a surplus which was equal to the aggregate of all the surpluses since confederation. This year he might equally have boasted that he had brought down a surplus which included not only last year's but all the surpluses of foregoing years since Canada was a nation. But he was singularly silent, because he knew that, while people were asking for bread, he was going to hand them a stone.
Everyone has been concerned with the rising cost of living. The government looked for a scapegoat and instituted the prices committee. As was suggested when the resolution was introduced, they have not called as a witness either the governor of the Bank of Canada or

the deputy minister of finance, who could well explain the inflationary background of rising prices due to the government's war fiscal policy. Nor have they sought to discover the influence of taxation on the cost of living, which would be a proper assignment for that committee.
All taxes, including personal income taxes to some extent, tend to find their way into the cost of the things we buy. Imagine, then, the influence on present-day costs of a government which takes in taxation alone $2,384 million out of a total national income of $10,820 million, or, as I mentioned, twenty-three cents out of every dollar earned. Put in another way it means that Mister Average-Canadian is working ten hours for Ottawa out of every forty hours he is employed. Add to that provincial and municipal taxes, and Mister Average-Canadian probably finds himself working a total of one and a half days for the state, leaving only three and a half days to meet his direct family expenditures.
The surplus last year was equal to the total of personal income tax payments by all Canadians, and yet not even a gesture of thanks was made by this government. The rate of taxation is still extraordinarily high. In the personal income tax field, after the minimum and niggardly exemptions, the first $100 earned is taxed ten per cent; when $500 is earned the rate is twenty per cent; if $8,500 is earned the rate is thirty-five per cent; and when $17,000 is earned the rate is fifty per cent, from which poiDt it rises to eighty per cent, and if there is investment income in excess of $1,800, there is an additional four per cent.
The smallness of the exemptions and the rates of taxation speak for themselves, and one need hardly refer to the fact that the rate at the peak of taxation a few- years ago was but a few per cent higher than what we are faced with today. It suffices to say that in the peak year of 1944-45 income taxation produced $768 million, and in 1947-48, $660 million, or a reduction from the wartime peak of a mere fourteen per cent. Whatever the reductions may have been, they are a far cry from 1939, when the total personal income tax taken by the government was $61,000,000. We still have an increase of 1,100 per cent and are apparently not entitled to any reduction.
The minister mentioned that he was budgeting for production. The facts indicate that he is budgeting for a continuance of the high cost of living, which is not to be confused with inflation. How any government thinks it can extract twenty-three cents from every dollar of national income and not force prices

The Budget-Mr. Jackman
up is beyond imagination. The fact that the government have just removed the eight per cent sales tax on certain processed foods is an indication that in their heart of hearts they know that taxation is directly contributory to the high cost of living.
In view of what I have said, what does the minister mean when he said there have already been three substantial reductions in the personal income tax, and it "offers no serious impediment to work or initiative-at least none that could be removed by any further reasonable reduction". His qualification would seem to admit that any taxation interferes with incentive and therefore with production.
1 think he is right up to a point, but he has lost his sense of balance when it comes to calculating the effect of restoring even a moderate amount of incentive. Incentive-destroying taxes are the greatest sin against the financial integrity and the productive efforts of our country. If given reasonable incentive and rewards, Canadians will work like beavers preparing for a long winter.
One of the amusing and amazing things about the minister's budget is that the extraordinary amount of surplus last year, $670 million, was unexpected. But once having got it into his hands, he finds a thousand and one reasons why he should keep it there, and why this method of painful extraction should be continued indefinitely.
There is nothing new in the idea of a cyclical budget. It has been practised by people with common horse sense for at least five thousand years. Now, however, the individual is not to be allowed to keep what he earns, but the state will keep it for him. The state, not the individual, will provide for the proverbial rainy day. It never has in the past.
The unexpected size of the surplus is a reflection on the government's estimates and the whole theory of a managed economy. One would think dire calamity would happen if the government did not retain last year's surplus and budget for another one. Once having gotten a surplus, even by chance, and finding that the people have not been forceful enough in asking for some relief, the government have thought up ways and means of keeping from the people their own money. The government have therefore trotted out the idea of cyclical budgets on the basis of taxing for a surplus in good times so that they can spend more of your money than they take away from you in bad times. In the meantime the individual is lost sight of.
Are Canadians not to be trusted to look after their own earnings, or must the government do it for them? Who built Canada 5849-277
up? Was it a race of foolish, improvident people or a race of pioneering, hard-working, thrifty, God-fearing people? Money will burn a hole in the government's pocket just the same way as if you take a spare $100 out of your bank and carry it around loose in your pocket.
Are we to build up the state and forget the individual? Never can you have a prosperous state without a prosperous people. Do Canadians want the state to look after all their housekeeping? Do men and women want to rely solely on the state for their jobs and for their old age? No, they want an opportunity to provide for themselves. They do not want to be spoon-fed like a baby, but rather they want a chance to manage their own affairs like men. Anyone who has been familiar with government spending knows that the individual usually obtains much better value for every dollar spent than does some government agency with its tremendous overhead and its lack of regard for the sweat and toil which savings represent. It is high time that the reins of government were taken out of the hands of a bureaucracy and were returned to parliament and the people.
No consideration was given to allowing the wage earner or the farmer,-again with his own money-any relief to meet the rising cost of living. With an amazing and unexpected surplus, the least that might have been expected was some increase in the present tax exemption levels of $750 for a single person and $1,500 for a married couple. It has always beggared the imagination of the speaker that any government should place a direct tax which lowers the standard of living below the minimum level to which Canadians with their skill and resources are entitled. With the cost of living increased from 130 in April, 1947, to 153 in 1948, or eighteen per cent, one would have expected that a trustee of the people's money would afford them some small measure of relief, despite three trifling reductions since the peak of wartime taxation. Perhaps a change of trustees is long overdue.
The ability of the government to concede and the need of the people for some increase in tax exemptions are so clear that one can only surmise that any reasonable government would have been willing to grant some concession, had it not been for an administrative bureaucracy that just did not want to go to the trouble and bother of changing the income tax forms.
The only managed economies which we have known in recent times were the national socialist regime under Hitler, the fascist
The Budget-Mr. Jackman

corporate state under Mussolini, and communism under Stalin. Once you put the money managers in the saddle, their every excuse for failure is "give me a little more power; let me tighten the reins a bit more and use a little more severe bit in the mouth of the once gallant horse." Finally, t'he animal is completely tamed because it has lost its spirit; but it does not win any more races and it does not perform in the way it used to. The spirit of enterprise is lost and a general lowering of the standard of living is t'he result.
Surely this continent has seen enough of managed economy when the Roosevelt pumppriming experiment was unsuccessfully tried in the United States, and billions of dollars were thrown away in an attempt to get the United States economy moving. Let me tell the minister that all the cyclical budgets in the world and all the pump-priming in the ocean are not worth a nickel as compared with the force of men's fears and hopes.
The minister talks about iuflation and how his present action in denying the people what is rightfully theirs is best for them. The candy, which is not the minister's candy after all, is to be handed out one stick at a time and the child is not allowed to have the whole bag in his own possession. But the minister overlooks the fact that he himself may lose the bag. The 'house might have been more interested if the minister had explained that the government itself is responsible for inflation; that inflation is due to nothing more or less than the wartime fiscal and monetary policy of his government; and I am not criticizing him at the moment for that. He might also have pointed out that too much money is just as inflationary, whether spent by an individual for something useful and where value is received, or whether spent by the government for something likely a good deal less useful and likely where value will not be received. In an interesting speech by Courtland Elliott, C.B.E., who has the happy advantage of both a sound theoretical training and a practical background, he has this to say:
The fact is that government expenditures and their financing are the most potent inflationary forces in the world today. Yet having absorbed the shock of present tax rates, we seem to be willing to accept the delusion that taxes cannot be reduced because of inflationary measures.
I venture the prediction that when times change we shall accept the explanation that taxes cannot be reduced materially because we shall then be in a deflationary period and relief and public works expenditures will require high taxes.
It is incredible to anyone with a knowledge of government ways and particularly of political pressures that any government could be

a saver of money over a long term. It might have been possible at some time in our history, but not since governments have allowed themselves to be held responsible for the prosperity of the people. Moreover, it is hard enough to save money when one has worked for it with the sweat of one's brow. But as far as the government goes, there is a saying, "Easy come, easy go."
It was also interesting to hear the minister say:
In any case, once full employment is reached, as it was last year, any expansion in total output is bound to be limited and gradual.
This is a nice pretty statement which just does not mean a thing. I can think of no economic group in the country that would not produce more if they did not have the burden of an additional rate of taxation on additional production. What has happened to the minister's clear thinking when in his budget of 1947 he said:
It is the high marginal rate of tax on additional earnings that discourages additional work, enterprise and initiative and consequently we must aim in our reductions at cutting down these marginal rates of tax.
There is not a farmer member of this house who does not know that more milk and butter could be produced but for the discouraging effect of higher taxes on additional production. The same applies to cattle and hog raisers; and indeed I am told that good hired men will not even work for bosses who make income tax deductions from their pay. The result is that the farmer pays the tax himself. The hired man is interested, as is everyone else, in take-home pay, and if it is not high enough he strikes for more. The same thing applies in our cities to household assistants. We would have more houses built if carpenters, plumbers and plasterers were not faced with incentive-destroying taxation. There is no need to stop at the artisan classification. Nurses often have carefully figured out just how much income takes them into the next higher bracket or causes their husbands to lose their marital exemption. The same goes for professional men, who now indulge in long, extended vacations because of the economic futility of working additional hours. What is the use of working an extra evening in the week if the bulk of the earnings is to be taken away in taxation? If we lived in a vacuum the minister's contention might be right; but we do not, and it might be a good thing if he had a little more time to go around and learn something about the problems of his constituents in St. Antoine-Westmount.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
He gets around quite a bit.

The Budget-Mr. Jackman

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, it is surprising that his majority the last time was only sixty. Continued high taxation has led and will lead to demands for higher wages, to strikes, and to a lessening of production. Only recently it was noted in the newspapers that the medical doctors had increased their fees. All taxation-and this goes for income tax, too- eventually enters into the cost of the things our people buy. It is hard enough to get people to work for themselves, much less for the government.
Another point on which there is some confusion, Mr. Speaker, is this. Full employment does not mean full production. Many times in Canada's history we have had full employment when production, both in agriculture and in industry, was but a bare fraction of what it is today. Doctor Mackintosh of Queen's university recently pointed out that the gross output in Canada in 1938 was $5-1 billion and that this year it will exceed $14 billion. Our population has not changed substantially in that period. After allowing for the rise in prices, the increase in real output per capita is about thirty-five per cent. The output of all workers has been increased by the use of more power, capital equipment and management. With some incentive to businessmen, particularly owners of small businesses, to acquire the machines, and with some incentive to the workers to operate the machines to the full, then we can expect a still further and immediate substantial increase in production. Full employment and full production are not necessarily the same thing. The brawn, muscle and skill of the farmer or workman when directing the power-driven machine has made possible the steadily rising standard of living on this continent. We need to encourage, by restoring incentive, owners to venture forth and workers to put forth their best efforts, so that the national pie will be greater and the slice of each will be larger.
The minister says that "to slash our taxes now would fasten controls more securely on our national life." The opinion of many is that if we do not restore incentive and production the government will always find reasons for retaining controls to regulate the distribution of scarcity. Again, it was interesting to hear the minister say:
It has done what a government could do to meet inflationary pressure by the most fundamental method, that is, by stimulating increased production to satisfy excessive demands.
Later on he said:
On our taxation side, our policy has been to reduce our taxes where they were impeding work and production.
What a change in his thinking from last year; or shall we say, what wonders were worked by a small dose of Abbott's relief remedy! The small cut in taxation which worked this miraculous cure was so powerful that it must have been encased in an atomic bomb!
The minister directed attention to our national expenditures, and mentioned particularly the large amount that went into new construction, industrial plants and equipment, public utility projects and housing. I shall not criticize the government unduly for its policy of double depreciation. At some time in the life of a plant the cost is allowed to be written off for replacement purposes, and the fact that the depreciation was accelerated does not necessarily mean that the total tax take is less. I would point out, however, that the policy of double depreciation was another example of faulty planning. Hindsight shows it to have been totally unnecessary and to have aggravated the inflationary tendencies aready existing in our economy. Had we needed to create employment, it would have been a fine thing, but once again our economic managers saw dimly through dark-coloured glasses. The effect of upping our dollar from 90 cents to 100 cents U.S. also had the effect of encouraging manufacturers to embark on extensive capital improvement programs requiring the importation of American machinery, and this at a time when we did not need to encourage expansion on t'he part of anyone. As a result of accepting the advice of those who hold themselves out as expert managers of our economy, the minister was able to say:
Our forecast proved to be much too conservative; prices, wages, profits and expenditures all increased much more than we anticipated.
On all four counts the government was wrong. In his reference to the rapidly rising price level in Canada, the minister said the adjustment was inevitable but was made easier because of the government's action on July 5, 1946, in restoring the Canadian dollar to parity with the LTnited States dollar. Of course he does not think a ten per cent increase in prices would have discouraged the buying of American products by Canadians. Many of us think otherwise. Now that he is in a distressing predicament in regard to United States exchange, having wilfully lost the country's reserves, he imposes embargoes and import restrictions. Just yesterday morning a fresh batch of import restrictions were announced by his colleague the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). This is just another example of how one control breeds another, until the camel is occupying the tent and the
The Budget-Mr. Jackman

Arab is outside shivering in the cold of the desert night. Furthermore the Minister of Finance Should write it down in his copy book that Canadians will not permanently accept a lower standard of living than Americans, and it would be interesting to know what his government has done to increase the purchase of Canadian products by the United States. Indeed I should have thought at least half the cabinet would have been in Washington in an endeavour to increase our trade with that country, particularly to have them buy more of our products.
As to the corporation tax, little need be said at this moment. Before the war it was eighteen per cent; and I hope my hon. friends of the C.C.F. will remember that. It is now thirty-five per cent or thirty-seven per cent, depending upon the province in which the corporation carries on its business. It is true that the excess profits tax has been done away with as of the end of last year, but its place has been taken in large part by the increased normal corporation tax rate. I do not know whether anyone thinks corporations are soulless treasure houses that have some endless means of paying taxes, but one might as well realize that corporation taxes, like all other taxes, rapidly become absorbed in the cost of the articles corporations make and sell.
If I may refer again to the theory of the cyclical budget, the minister has pointed out the advisability of saving in good times to tide over bad times. If it works that way, the principle is sound. But the political philosophy to which most of the members of this house subscribe is that the state is but the sum total of its people, and I for one would prefer to see our people with some reserve themselves, so that like sensible human beings they could have some fat on their bones to tide themselves over the more difficult times. Again I would reiterate that a pump-priming has never been successful in any country and that individuals are entitled to put something by for their own rainy day in the same way as a veteran is entitled to save some of his money, so that he may make a down payment on the small home he so badly needs; or a farmer or a businessman is entitled to retain some of his earnings to pay off his borrowings. Parents are likewise entitled to put something by for the education of their children, to say nothing of their own old age.
The minister also mentioned as a reason for a cyclical budget that we might be confronted with a large increase in expenses for national defence. To quote him, he said:
Otherwise we would have to add to the other disturbing effects of an expanded defence pro-

gram the complications of sudden inflationary expenditures or sudden increases in taxes. A substantial surplus will help to keep our powder dry.
To this I may only add that what is needed to deliver the goods is a new powder monkey.
In the last war we froze our civilian economy and the wages of our workers in civilian production. In order to expand our war production, wages of workers in war industry rose to new high levels, so that boys of sixteen and seventeen found themselves earning much more than their fathers whose wages were frozen. It was, of course, necessary to drain off some of this surplus purchasing power, because civilian production could not be expanded. I wonder wffiat is to become of our economy and our freedom if, on top of the present high levels of taxation, we had to increase, because of armament expenditures, our general level of taxation. If we were fighting for our freedom against a foreign foe we should surely lose it to those who were regulating our internal economy. For this reason, if for no other, the minister should endeavour to cut down government expenses and reduce our level of taxation, so that it is not only bearable but able to stand the imposition of wartime taxation.
In his third reason for a cyclical budget or a managed economy, the minister stated:
Tax reductions would add nothing to production.
In this, as I have already stated, I think he is immeasurably and entirely wrong. He made a reference to certain unknown strong or fortunate groups who could look after themselves if the inflation he feared took hold. May I say to him that, like war, inflation is a national calamity and I know of no one who does not fear it as one should fear the devil.
The one small bone that Mother Hubbard was able to find in the cupboard was the elimination of the sales tax on processed foods. Nothing contributed to the rising cost of living more than the pyramided sales tax, and I think it was a surprise to many that this tax was applied against a great list of food products that did not happen to be sold in their raw state, such as cereals, all packaged foods, all canned goods, preserves, jams and jellies, and all smoked meats such as sausages, bacon and ham. It had always been understood that the sales tax did not apply to two of the three great essentials of life-food and shelter-and now that understanding is virtually a reality. For this I congratulate the minister.
It is interesting to note, however, that he says that this relief from taxation will create little additional inflationary pressure. I agree

The Budget-Mr. Mclvor
with him, but not more so than I would agree with him if he were to reduce taxation generally.
Time will not permit me to go into the comparison which the minister made of United States taxes with our own, but I would point out that the tables which he placed on Hansard clearly show that our own system of taxation is anti-social. The single man is taxed more in the United States, whereas the married couple are taxed more in Canada. I congratulate the minister for granting an additional exemption to people over sixty-five years. It was long overdue.
As to succession duties, I should like to say just one word. While I have not had an opportunity to examine the effect of the changes, I am one of those who believe that succession duties are one of the fairest forms of taxation. Large inheritances make for inequality of opportunity among our citizens, and substantial succession duties provide a desirable source of revenue because they have not the objection of incentive-destroying taxes.
As a final justification for withholding from the Canadian people a substantial part of what they create and earn, the minister said:
The activities and scope of government in Canada have been extended by popular consent and indeed by popular demand. Parliament and the government have a wider responsibility than before the war, particularly in the field of economic affairs.
This cannot be gainsaid, but any government which is worthy of the name should be at some pains to point out to the people that the money which goes to finance social services is not created out of thin air. Because of the extent of our social services, no longer is the money taken from one group and paid over to another group of our people. Every family in the land is subject to direct and indirect taxation for the express purpose of providing these social services, although many people have the feeling that someone else is paying the shot. True leadership would indicate to our people that the extension of many social services simply means that they will be taxed in order that the government may provide them rather than that they will be able to save in order to provide the services for themselves. The money will in either case come out of their own hard-earned savings.
Already taxation, federal, provincial and municipal, is taking close on to a third of what all our people are producing. This is a startling amount in comparison with pre-war figures. If it goes on far enough with a few per cent added each year it will soon bring us up to fifty per cent of our earnings being
retained by the government. We shall have lost our freedom as individuals and be subject to some form of state socialism or of outright communism. Again, revolutions can be silent as well as violent.
Canada was built up on the principle of individual liberty, and if one is not permitted to have some financial reserves he loses his economic freedom. The liberties which we hold most sacred are lost to us because we are subject to political domination at every turn. It is my belief that we shall do better, that we shall be more creative, that there will be more to divide and distribute among all if free enterprise is allowed to function and the individual is permitted to retain his economic freedom with which goes his political liberty.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have much pleasure in congratulating the minister upon his budget. My first reason for offering congratulations is that, notwithstanding the headlines and prophecies of federal members and others, there was not one bit of leakage until the minister announced his budget. As one lion.. member said, "Only God and Abbott knew what was in the budget." Considering the pressure, considering the telegrams and letters which he received, I think this is proof that he is a man of stability and one who can keep his own counsel.
This proves that those who prophesied a great reduction in income tax were false prophets, and I would give a warning now to those who are beginning to make prophecies about the next budget, that it will be an election budget. This means, I suppose, that there will be no tax reductions, that the budget will be just as tight as this one. If it is, it will certainly be a feather in the cap of the minister. It is easy to do the popular thing. I listened, for instance, to members of the opposition urging that old age pensions should be increased to $60 a month, and I think they should. If I were an old man and had nothing to live on but $60 a month I would not be able to go very often to the picture shows, and I certainly would be glad that I did not smoke a pipe.
The hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Matthews) struck a very fine note when he said, in effect, that this was a good business budget. When I contract a debt and sign a note, Mr. Speaker, I am in duty bound to take up the note and pay the debt, and when we realize that, according to the hon. member for Brandon, one billion dollars has been paid off the national debt within two
The Budget-Mr. Mclvor

years, meaning a reduction of $30,000,000 in interest charges, that is something for which the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is to be commended.
Another thing for which I commend the Minister of Finance is for not making promises. It is so easy to make promises. So many men in different walks of life have found themselves in difficulties because they could not fulfil their promises and somebody took legal action against them for breach of promise. You cannot do that against our Minister of Finance. The only man who has made a promise to this house is the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), and he has made a good one. The hospitals are finding it very difficult to carry on and to find sufficient beds for their patients, and the Prime Minister has promised $30,000,000 to help them. That will be very helpful indeed to those who are ill.
Another thing upon which I congratulate the minister is this, and I was reminded of it by a letter that I received yesterday from somebody at Fort William who has found that this budget makes a difference in her grocery bills. She says that this is the first time she has experienced a little relief from high taxation, and she mentions a reduction of five cents a pound on ham and bacon and says that her grocery bill will be smaller So that is the best kind of tax reduction for her.
The minister may be up against it a little, because he has given some relief in his budget to the men and women who are over sixty-five years of age, for he may find that there are more people over sixty-five years of age in Canada than he thought there were before this budget came into existence.
I would have liked to see a reduction made in the sales tax for the relief of our retailers, and I would also have liked to see the excise tax reduced. But there is a long year ahead of us and many things can happen in that year. I notice that the tax on silver-plated articles has been reduced. I would like to see watches put on the free list. Watches are used universally and are a necessity. I would also tell the minister that he should give some relief in the matter of wedding rings. They, too, should be put on the free list. Imagine a young man getting married and not being able to buy a wedding ring, and then two or three weeks afterwards his wife goes to a social gathering and it is seen that she has not got a wedding ring on! The Minister of Justice might say that was the beginning of a divorce, but of course that is not always true.
Another thing I would like to see is some relief for the mining industry. I have received a number of committees from the mining industries at the head of the lakes, and I

would like to see a little more help given to our mining industry. When we could not get jobs for our men during the depression I remember how we used to go to these mine operators and how they helped out our unemployed. I am sure the minister will take this into his sympathetic consideration.
I would also like to express the thanks of our community to the government for having increased by twenty-five per cent the pension that is paid to those who fought and risked their lives for us. That will come out of the surplus for next year perhaps. I think it is the absolute duty of the dominion government to look after these men, and the women too, who gave their best and came back less fit than they were before to do their life's work.
When the Prime Minister promised assistance amounting to $30,000,000 to the provinces, I was very well pleased because we in Fort William need hospital aid. If a certain government is elected in Ontario I expect we shall get about $300,000, but if another government is elected maybe we shall not get it. When I see beds in the halls of hospitals, outside the maternity ward, the children's ward and other wards, I say it is high time that our governments got together, and I thank the Prime Minister for this encouragement. When the provinces make their recommendations to (he dominion government they will get their share, but it is necessary, of course, for the provinces and the dominion government to get together.
I should like to say in closing that in Canada we have more nearly realized than any other country, including Russia and even New Zealand, the four freedoms. Where is the man today who cannot get a job? I know some people may have difficulty in getting work because of poor health or accident or for some other reason; but there is no reason why, if a man is willing to take the first thing that comes, as you and I did, Mr. Speaker, and work at that until he gets something better, all our people can be employed, and that makes Canada the greatest country on earth.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the few remarks which I shall make this afternoon will, I hope, be constructive and mean something in the future as to the manner in which the government brings down its budget and perhaps also as to the manner in which this budget will be dealt with at a later stage by the house this session.
I heartily agree with the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that in good times we should budget for a surplus. As long ago as 1791, Alexander Hamilton, who was perhaps the

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
first and leading economist of his time in any country, said this in his report to congress:
As the vicissitudes of nations beget a perpetual tendency to the accumulation of debt, there ought to be in every government a perpetual, anxious and unceasing effort to reduce that which at any time exists as fast as shall be practicable consistently with integrity and good faith.
From that time until the present it has been the hope, the desire and the aim of every country in its budget to have a surplus in good times so as to be able to meet the deficits which are bound to come in the bad times which have always followed. In the United States in the time of Hamilton they had a debt of S77 million. This was progressively reduced until in 1812, when the war with Great Britain broke out, the debt was only $45 million. It was increased by that war to S133 million. This again was reduced until 1851 when it stood at $68 million.
The civil war, which was perhaps the greatest war of all time up to that date, increased the debt of the United States to $2,756 million, which for a people of thirty million, was not anything like the debt which we are now bearing in Canada, but which at the time was thought to be almost unbearable. However, the United States faced the problem, and in the year 1893 this had been reduced from $2,756 million to $838 million. Because of the depression which then arose, it stood still until the beginning of the great war.
The first great war raised the debt of the United States to about $25 billion, which, at the time, was thought to be almost an astronomical figure. They again attempted to reduce it and in fifteen years had reduced it by $9 billion to about $16 billion. Then came the depression of the thirties and the debt kept going up until in 1936 it amounted to $34 billion. In fact it doubled in those depression years.
We all know that the last war increased the debt of the United States to such an extent that it is now about $269 billion. At the present time they are doing what they can to reduce this debt.
I must say that in the last year the United States had an income of about $40 billion. While they had expenditures of $42 billion, in that $42 billion they include all loans which they made to other countries. As I recall it, about $7 billion of the $42 billion is made up of loans made to European countries. That is why I am going to say that in Canada actually we have no surplus. It is true that, because of the bookkeeping methods we have adopted, the minister shows a surplus of some $450 million or $500 million, but certain things
do not appear in the expenditures. For instance, they show only $75 million toward a sinking fund. We must remember that during the last year we advanced to other countries the sum of about $646 million. This advance of $646 million was one of the main factors which produced large incomes in the country. It is fair to say that of this $646 million, which was spent in loans to other countries, and out of which goods were provided, perhaps as much as half, or over $300 million, would be taken back by the government in the form of taxes. This is more likely to be the case, because that extra amount of money which was obtained by the people would be added on to the ordinary income of the people and would place them in higher income brackets. Therefore I think the Minister of Finance in his budgeting should have allowed about $300 million-which is about one-half of what the United States allowed-as an expenditure during the last year. If that were done the surplus would, of course, practically disappear.
It is unfortunate that the minister, in some of his talks to the newspaper men last year, referred to a surplus. As a result of that, a great deal of adverse criticism was voiced. Actually, if the figures had been put on the same basis as they are placed in the United States there would not be a surplus at all, but a deficit.
I have looked into the figures of this year, and I have been unable to find about $50,000,000 which was voted to the provinces of Saskatchewan, British Columbia, Alberta and Manitoba last year. To my way of thinking, that is as much an expense as if it were paid out of your pocket, because actually before that time it had been carried as an asset of government. The writing off of it amounted to an expenditure. I spent some time looking, but I have not been able to find where the payment appears in the accounts as presented by the government. I very much doubt whether it appears anywhere. That would reduce the surplus also.
It is of great importance that we have a surplus in good times, because of the method of showing the receipts from income tax, corporation taxes and other taxes. I wrote a letter to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), and he quite frankly replied that so far as the receipts for any fiscal year are concerned it means all the money that is paid in for that year. He refers to an example I cited and says:
In the example which you have cited, if a taxpayer paid his 1946 tax on the first of March, 1947, it would be considered as 1946-47 revenue. If a similar payment, even although it were on account of 1946 tax, were made on the 15th
The Budget-Mr. McMaster

day of April, l!/47, then that payment would be considered as 1947-48 revenue. The taxation year for which a tax may be paid has no bearing whatever on the fiscal year to which the revenue is credited.
It may be said' that for statistical purposes separate records are maintained with respect to the amount of tax collected for any particular calendar year. This is entirely separate from the amounts which are considered as revenue for the fiscal year.
Therefore one might expect that if a depression came along the moneys which may be received for any year may be very much less than the money actually paid for that year; because of that, I say the listed receipts for any year do not actually give the amount of money that was paid for that year; and for that reason also the surplus shown is uncertain. It should be scrutinized closely and should not be accepted as the definite amount of any surplus.
The question arises, how do you produce a real surplus? Of course there are only two ways by which a government can produce a surplus. They are similar ways to that by which any person in private life could produce one. You must either increase your revenue or reduce your expenditure.
I should like to deal for a moment with the question of reduction of expenditures since I would be the last person to suggest to the Minister of Finance that he should increase his revenue in any way, because the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman) has shown that we are now paying twenty-three per cent of our total income in taxes. When we take into consideration provincial and municipal taxes the amount is probably thirty-three per cent. We must remember that everybody is not paying thirty-three per cent. Some people pay no taxes; others are paying ten per cent; still others are paying fifteen per cent, and so on, but some are paying seventy-five per cent or eighty per cent. But if the total amount of taxes paid is thirty-three per cent of the total income, then I believe the future of our country looks very bleak indeed. I recall that we used to talk about England as the country of high taxes. As I recall it, the highest amount paid there was thirty-six per cent of the total national income. We all know what conditions were there at that time. If these conditions obtained in Canada in ordinary times it would impose a very great burden indeed upon the Canadian people.
The minister may ask me how I would reduce expenditures. I say to the minister that expenditures must be reduced. Actually a great deal of them cannot be reduced. I recognize as well as the minister does that the

interest on the national debt must be paid. I can understand and appreciate the fact that we are paying a very low rate of interest on that indebtedness; that the amount might be increased; that, instead of being $450 million, it might easily be $550 million.
I recognize at once that, since we have started to pay family allowances, we shall continue to do so. It would be a tremendous undertaking on the part of any government to change that. I understand that our veterans must be looked after, and all these uncontrollable expenditures must be taken care of, but there are other things that the minister must face. I went to some pains today to look at the increase in expenditures from 1938 to last year, and in some cases the present year, and I find that those expenditures which are purely ordinary administration and departmental expenditures, could be kept down more than they are.
We are going ahead, putting more people on the payroll, paying them more money, and while it may be good for these people, I can only say to the minister that if he keeps on in that way he is doing what the C.C.F. wants to do. He is putting everyone on the payroll. You cannot spend yourself into prosperity by having a lot of people on the payroll, any more than you can drink yourself into prosperity. The minister must face these things.
I would point out some of the departments in which there has been a tremendous and unjustified increase. Let me take first agriculture, and I am speaking now of the administration end of it. I begin with 1938-39, which was perhaps a normal year. We shall be lucky if we ever have an average year as good as that in the rest of our lives. I do not know whether we shall have any better times than in the past, but I do not think the millennium is coming soon. It is rather the other way around; it is farther away. In 1938-39-I will say 1938 for the sake of brevity'-we spent in agriculture for administration $9,527,000. In the year 1948-49, as set out in the estimates, that is now $18,000,000.
