subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In external affairs in
1939, when we were an ordinary country minding our own business, we spent $1,057,000, and for the next year we shall spend, as provided by the estimates, $9,777,000. It has gone up 900 per cent. It seems to me that Canada is going beyond the point it should go in these expenditures. I realize that a great deal of this is caused by present conditions. Maybe a million of it has to do with the united nations and perhaps half a million with other organizations which are more or less international in character; but I still say that we are spending altogether too much on external affairs, and I suggest that we can reduce the taxes on our people if we do something in this connection.
I come now to something I do not understand, and that is the annual amortization of bonds and commissions. In 1938 we spent practically $5,000,000, and that has gone up to $8,000,000.
In the finance department, which is a large department, I know, administration cost about $3,500,000 in 1938, and that has gone up to over $20,000,000.
In the fisheries department there has been an increase from $2,036,000 to $5,996,000. After all, while we can do something for the fishermen, we may have to do something more than that for them in bad times, because they have had bad times in the past and may have bad times in the future. Perhaps an expenditure of about $3,000,000 might be helpful to them in bad times, more helpful than such an expenditure now on something that is not directly beneficial to them at the present moment.
The justice department has gone up from $2,748,000 to $3,601,000, which is not much.
The labour department has risen from $788,000 to $2,295,000. In that connection I would refer not only to the administration of the labour department but to unemployment insurance. The rather considerable sum of $18,000,000 is paid out in salaries. It may be a large department; and that sum has nothing to do with the contribution of $17,000,000 which the government is making to the unemployment fund. It strikes me that $18,000,000 is a very considerable sum to pay for carrying on the administration work of that department; that is, the unemployment insurance department.
The House of Commons has gone up from $1,800,000 to $3,878,000. Immigration has gone up from $1,335,000 to $3,788,000. Indian affairs has gone up from $5,305,000 to over $7,000,000. Lands, parks and forests, special
projects, has gone up from $2,249,000 to $5,738,000. The post office has gone from $35,000,000 to over $67,000,000. Public printing and stationery has gone up slightly.
I now come to public works. We have been talking about budgeting for bad times, and many people in the past have said quite truly that all public works should be left if possible until bad times come. In that connection I should like to read something that might be helpful to the government. It appears in a book by Erik Lindtahl, written some time ago. It is in regard to budgeting for a surplus in good times. He says: "The benefits of so doing are: (1) Financial gains would accrue to the state and to the local authorities through a reduction in the average level of costs for construction work, etc. (2) There would be less unemployment and better utilization of production capacity during depression years. (3) There would be more stable prices and less violent economic fluctuations owing to the monetary effect of the recurrent under-andover balancing of the budget through adjustment of public expenditures between boom and depression years."
We have heard about cycle years and their effect on budgeting, and this writer points out that the trade cycle should not be allowed to affect normal public activities. That is why I say that it would be no kindness to the people employed by the government in these administrative jobs if we were to dispense with their services during bad times, and yet we cannot keep them there in ordinary times. I suggest in fairness to them, that their services should be dispensed with as far as possible in good times and, if possible, they should be taken on in bad times when they need the jobs. Public works should be undertaken in depression years.
Too much has been done in these late years. The tax burden should be lighter during depression and heavier during boom. I agree with the minister in that regard, and I was moved to read that statement of Mr. Lindtahl because public works have risen from $20 million in 1938-39 to a total of $59 million in the present estimates. I would suggest to the minister that a great deal of this work should be left until such time as it can be done to greater advantage and with less expense to the country, and so that the money would be distributed among a larger Amber of people.
I have made some suggestions in a business way, and I hope that even politically they will bear results, even from the standpoint of those who might put them into force.
I would suggest something about revenues. As I have said, perhaps the revenues are high, but new revenues can be obtained from those

The Budget-Mr. McMasttr
who now ecsape taxation and who are able to pay. In the last analysis, the money should be obtained from those who are most able to pay, and I suggest that there is a large field of unearned increment that lias not been taxed.
When I say this I do not want anyone to say that if you allow for unearned increment you have to allow for losses, because I will not admit that for a moment. The United States lost revenue because they allowed the losses of stocks to be set off against gains in stock. That is not right; it is not fair; it is not necessary, and I am not suggesting that that should be done.
But there is a great deal of unearned income. One reason for that is this high income tax. Of course I am not a prophet. I am not a great businessman either or I would not make this statement, because it might have some adverse effect. But I am sure that prices of many stocks are kept up today in the hope that somebody will make some money out of those stocks, which money will be untaxed. What these people want is to get some money that is not taxed, because they do not want to pay taxes any more than anyone else does; and in the case of rich people, the taxes are fairly high. I would suggest, for instance, that that would be one of the most effective ways of stopping inflation.
If there is anything in the world that I want, it is to stop inflation. I hitched my political life to the promise that I would do my best to stop inflation. During the war the government did a good job in keeping down inflation, but I am not so proud of what they have done since. In some cases I believe that where they should have been firm, they yielded; it looks as though inflation may get the better of things. I know there are a great many people who are gambling everything on inflation. They are buying everything of a tangible nature. They actually think the same thing will happen here as happened in Germany; therefore they will buy something tangible, and the other people who have investments in government bonds or mortgages will be paid off with worthless pieces of paper. One of the ways to stop that is to tax unearned increment.
I suggest that the sooner the government get their experts to work at that, the better it will be. so that something may be evolved. It cannot be all-inclusive. There would be many who would escape it, but it would, I believe, have a most salutary effect on stopping the rise in prices.
A few days ago I spoke about accelerated depreciation in speaking about housing. I do not intend to go over that again, but I shall simply say that what I placed on Hansard at 
pages 36S9 to 3691 inclusive, I stand by. I did not intend to say anything about this accelerated depreciation, but I believe that it was allowed at a bad time. I believe it had an inflationary tendency. I think the government themselves are to blame in that they set a date at which this allowance for depreciation must be spent. If they had put the date further ahead, I would not have felt so badly about it, although for the life of me I cannot see why these people perhaps should not pay their taxes the same as everybody else. I realize, as one of the other speakers has said, that this depreciation is only accelerated, but I think it should have been decelerated. It should have been put off until some later time. It was given, of course, for the reason mentioned by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). As mentioned in the book put out by the government, it was done so that the people could get the benefit during a period of high taxes and not have to pay high taxes; for in bad times, of course, when there were no excess profits or no profits, there is little or nothing to charge depreciation against.
I have said something about increasing the revenue. I think it can be increased in the manner I have mentioned by taxing unearned income and otherwise. Then we could decrease some of the revenue, because I believe the people in the lower income brackets are paying too much. I think everybody should bear a fair share of the burden, but the people in the lower income brackets are bearing their burden in paying the sales tax. I hope the government will go through that sales tax list and leave out many other articles. They can add something else on luxuries for those who can pay, but I would suggest that if possible they should remove from that list some other articles used by the people in the lower income brackets. After all, on the list are one or two things that go into the building of houses, which is important. The poor man must have a house. I do not, of course, deal with the whole list, but I should like the minister to do something for those people who are in the lower income tax brackets by removing that tax which is bad, which cannot be seen, and therefore probably arouses much less vocal opposition than does the income tax.
I think there should be a larger amount of exemption for each child. Inflationary prices affect the married man more than they do anybody else, because for every child he must buy clothes, shoes and other necessaries. The amount of inflation affects him in proportion to the number of children he has. If they have two children, they are affected to double the extent the married couple with no children, so that something should be allowed more than

The Budget-Mr. McMaster
the $100 now allowed. I should think this amount could quite easily be increased and shouild be increased perhaps in such a way that the people with greater wealth should not be able to take advantage of it. They can get along all right, and most of them have not many children anyway, so that it will not affect them so much.
Again I think the rates of income taxes that were manipulated a little, and helpfully, downward by the minister at the last session, could be still further decreased. I am willing to agree that everybody should have a sense of responsibility for the way in which the country's business is carried on, and nothing brings that to his mind more quickly than the fact that he has to pay something toward it, no matter how small may be the amount. I would suggest to the minister-and I shall be somewhat definite in my suggestion in this case-that where previously the tax was started at ten per cent-that is, on the first $100-it seems kind of hard that a man after he gets over a very limited income, should have to pay $10 on an additional $100 of income. That could be put down to, say $4 and then jumped up by $4 a hundred until it gets to twenty per cent. Maybe it could be jumped by $2 a hundred and go to a higher base. This tax is a great burden on the people who are in this low-income tax group. They could be given a sense of responsibility at not so great a price as they are paying at the present time. I would be quite willing and would suggest that this concession, causing as it does a loss of revenue, which goes all the way up the line, should not be available for those who have incomes of $5,000 or more. I realize as much as does the minister-and he has said so publicly-that every increase in exemption that we give to people in the lower income tax groups goes all the way up the line; and that for the rich people it means an exemption at the rate of perhaps fifty per cent or sixty per cent.
I now come to another point, and I have spoken about it quite often. I feel just as strongly as ever on the subject; and if I need any reason for bringing it up now, it is in the fourth clause of the resolution relating to income tax, where it is suggested that expenses be allowed to people in the transportation business and to others who are in the business of, I think the wording is, the sale of real estate or on commission. It struck me, when I read it, that it is a much restricted clause.

I think that was what was intended; it applies not only to those who are selling real estate, but to all commissions and otherwise. I would urge that whatever regulations are made, and whatever concessions are to be given, they should be put in a definite form. Definite regulations should be made, saying these people shall get exemption for stated reasons. These should be publicized, and the rulings made should be available to the people. They should know what exemptions everybody else is getting. When they make up their income tax, it is a worry to them when they do not know exactly what is intended to be allowed. I would suggest in this case, and in fact in all other cases where there is a discretion as to allowance, that it be made definite.
I want to read to the minister something which is applicable not only to his discretion in this case but to all other discretions under the income tax laws. These words were written longer ago than I had thought; they appear in chapter 45 of that famous book, "The Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire", by Gibbon:
The discretion of the judge . . .
In this case it is the minister.
... is the first engine of tyranny. The laws of a free people should foresee and determine every question that may probably arise in the exercise of power and the transactions of industry.
I suggest to the minister that he go to some pains in making regulations covering every point in his discretion; that these should be publicized, and that the results of any act or decision on his part should be made public.

subtopic: ORGANIZATIONS ADVOCATING OVERTHROW OP CONSTITUTED AUTHORITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose that all hon. members have one thing in common; without exception we are anti-communist. So we must persist in our
Criminal Code Amendment

constant opposition to the spread of communism, for no one in this country but communists wants communism to prosper. Personally I dislike and distrust communism because it is dictatorial, because it is tyrannical and because it is totalitarian. Others hate it for these as well as additional reasons. I think they are all good. In dealing with this subject, without reference to party I think this house can be divided into two groups. In my view one is effective and the other is less effective.
One of these groups comprises those whose anti-communism is emotional and whose tendency is to fight heresy with the weapons of repression. Their hatred of communism is not confined to religious grounds. There are those whose hatred of communism is based on economic beliefs; based, as a matter of fact, so little on religion that any deviation from what they call free enterprise is to them treason. There is room also for those who cherish a love of country above all that our divers religious and economic heritages may offer. So far as these people are concerned, the heresies are against the church, capitalism and patriotism, and they say the solution is repression.
There is another group whose hatreds are shared by all others but who prefer to fight on grounds of reason rather than emotion. They are prepared to strike at the root of the evil. This group sees communism as a revolutionary movement headed down a blind alley, but definitely the result of social causes which it feels it can remedy. Its weapons are the traditional freedoms and the progressive removal of social injustices, with which Canadian people thoroughly agree. These are not martial weapons, but these people feel that they will strip the enemy of their weapons at least. I believe that the strategy of this latter group will be more effective in defeating the common enemy of both groups.
When repression is proposed1, when the outlawing of the communist party reaches the point of vote in this House of Commons, I ask myself, and every member of the house must ask himself, whether the persecution of a revolutionary minority is the answer. I have searched history, and I find that all that such persecution achieves is the gratification of some less attractive impulses of the persecutors; and, what is far more important, the ultimate triumph of the persecuted.
Let us examine the history of our own country. In 1917 communist groups were banned in this country. In 1918, after the close of the war, the order banning them was repealed. In 1921 the communist party was formed; and in 1932 the party was made illegal under the infamous section 98 of the

criminal code, which by the way was rarely used. In 1936 that section was repealed. In 1940 the party was again made illegal in this country, and in 1945 the ban was removed from the communist party.
In the interval, in 1942, the party changed its name to Labour Progressive. Under the auspices of that name and in the midst of the kindliest feeling toward them when this country was concerned with our heroic ally- tanks for Russia, aid to Russia, Stalingrad, Uncle Joe and all that sort of thing-the party was able to elect some members to the city councils of Winnipeg and Toronto; they were able to elect a member of the board of control of Toronto. Later the people of Toronto woke up and did away with him nicely, democratically by the way. Members were elected to the Ontario legislature and, I believe to the Manitoba provincial legislature, and one member was elected to this House of Commons.
It seems obvious that the passing of a law does not do away with them. They now claim a membership of more than 23,000 in Canada. They may be just puffing in the usual manner, but on the other hand it cannot be denied that they have shown considerable strength in some of the industrial areas in Canada. It is also to be noted that Bulgaria, Yugoslavia, Poland and Hungary all passed laws to do away with communism. Look at them now. That is a fate which I should like to avoid.
Let us take a look at Italy. Twenty-seven years ago Mussolini outlawed the communist party and declared to the world that he had done away with it. Then came the war; he died and his regime fell. We found Italy swarming with communists; there were millions of them. Italy had to make a choice; she had either to outlaw the communist party or to defeat it by democratic processes. Italy decided to do it the hard way. She fought and she won. Although it was not a decisive victory, it was undoubtedly a decisive battle which now gives her the opportunity to strengthen her social defences.
Last week presidential primaries were held in the state of Oregon, Stassen and Dewey being the candidates. Stassen had preached the outlawing of the communist party, and Governor Dewey took him up on it, accepted his challenge, debated it nationally and locally. The people of Oregon spoke and Dewey was elected.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that no matter what action we take against the communist party today, we shall find that there will be a revolutionary left wing popping up the minute that conditions get difficult again and men begin to

Criminal Code Amendment
lose their jobs, and somebody behind a wicket says: All those who want relief will line up on the right.
I started out at the beginning by defining the emotional approach to anti-communism and I advocated the rational approach because, amongst those with the emotional approach, there are people with dangerous illusions. They tend to pin the red label on all those whose political positions veer a little left of centre or who do not agree with their own political views. This not only overrates the enemy, but alienates political allies. Let me give the house an example.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) spoke in this house a few days ago and outlined Canada's foreign policy. It was a magnificent report of the greatest significance to the nation. It was moderate, and it met with the approval not only of members of the house but of the general Canadian public. This is what he said:
Canada would play her full part in every movement to give substance to the conception of an effective system of collective security by the development of regional pacts.
Yet in some sections of the country we hear comments being made upon it such as this:
Brutally warlike and imperialistic.
Again:
The most dangerous proposals.
Again:
The most incendiary ideas.
That is the way in which the communists talk about our foreign policy. Yet is it fair to say that all people who use similar terms are also communists? If that is so, then I need only tell you, Mr. Speaker, that exactly these words were used by the Duplessis press in Quebec to describe the minister's speech. They are not communists; no one can suggest that. They may not be very bright, and they may be opposed to this government, but they are not communists. I merely point out the danger of condemning by association. Regrettably it springs from a tendency to hang the red label on people who are not guilty of it and from an eagerness to use the red label to discredit sometimes a trade union, sometimes a social movement or anything else of a progressive nature that appears within a greedy man's grasp.
I do not think we shall get anywhere in that way. Our attack on communism must be as realistic as the communist attacks which took Rumania, Bulgaria, Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia ; it must be tailored to the thinking of our own people, and it must be directed against the reds who are really communists. It must
not rest simply on the assertion: "No matter what it is doing to you, our way of life is best." That is not good enough.
If I may be personal, to me communists are not necessarily those from across the seas; they are not those who simply demand socialized medicine, or higher old age pensions, or the restoration of price controls. I do not think anyone could hold any such views after having been progressively the mayor of an industrial city, the minister of labour of our largest province, and the member representing a large working-class constituency.
No; communists, to me, are people. To me, a communist is a man who holds a certain card; just as a fellow-traveller is a man whom I suspect of holding a party card but of being too discreet to admit it. As human beings go, many of them are as you and I. They give to the poor; they love their children; they are well informed, and their personal lives are not unlike ours. The trouble is that they are fanatics, blind, unreasoning fanatics; and no one can convince me that fanatics are not potentially dangerous. They are prepared to use boldness and force, or stealth and cunning, whichever the situation calls for. It is a coldblooded brand of power politics, utterly ruthless and utterly merciless in its belief that the end justifies the means. Its end is world domination. Their loyalties lie outside the borders of this land, despite their parrot-like reiteration to the contrary. The single-track mind, whatever its terminus, is a menace to all of us whose preference is for individual freedom, for tolerance and a willingness to see two sides to most questions. It is a menace to the vast majority of Canadians.
We have a criminal code for those who break the law. Let us apply the law for crimes they commit, not for ideas they have. I heartily approve strengthening the code to deal with these people and with subversive activities, but I am opposed to outlawing people for religious, political, social or economic views.
If, as has been suggested, we outlaw the communist party, or the Labour Progressive party, or whatever title it may appear under next, then I assure the house that our emotional impulse will bring forth hearty approval. This approval will come from, among others, the Labour Progressive party. We will drive them underground, which means that they will be given a stimulant toward organization, a badly needed provocation to party activity. They are born conspirators; they thrive on the cloak-and-dagger life; we will confer on them, by outlawing their party, a sense of romance that will attract converts, particularly immature converts, and what is more, we will toss into their lap the partisan
Criminal Code Amendment

halo. Out-in-the-open events often make them a little silly. But they are skilled tunnelers and sub-surface operators.
No, Mr. Speaker, let us be guided by reason rather than emotion. Communism is on the wane in this country mainly because people have jobs; they have enough to eat, and some of them are able to lay something aside for a rainy day. Some day I hope that the government gets around to finding a scientist who has a political turn of mind. I have a particular job for him. I hope that that political scientist will undertake the work and find out the relationship between calorie intake and communist enrolment in a given country. It seems to me that that is a study we have neglected.
I have said that the communists are on the way down. If anyone doubts that they are slipping, is there any' other explanation of their somewhat embarrassing support or attempted support of the C.C.F.? On every platform in this province, from every housetop the CLEF, are saying: We do not want their money; we do not want their support; we do not want their votes; we want no part of them. If they were an asset, that, to me, would not appear to be the normal reaction.
Where is their influence in this country? They have no representatives in the House of Commons. I am even surer that they have no representatives in the Senate. In so far as the legislatures are concerned, the communists have a few members in the province of Ontario, and I think one in the province of Manitoba; but their members are known, tagged and minimized. In the municipal councils they may have one here or there, but they are overwhelmed by numbers. And mind you, Mr. Speaker, the only way that they are able to elect members to these various legislative bodies is that there is a great deal of inertia amongst our own people. Where we find seventy-five per cent of the people voting, they have not a chance.
Someone may say that they have influence in the administrative offices of this country. I doubt that. We have had reason to believe that if they were there, they were cleaned out. They certainly are not in our police departments; they certainly are not in our armed services. I do not believe that they have any great influence in this country.
Communism can become important, but only when the masses of the people have been driven into despair by hunger-that is what happened in eastern Europe-or into a mistrust of democracy itself-that is what happened in Czechoslovakia. We in Canada can certainly produce a revival of communism only

if unemployment is permitted to rise again, or if we drive the communist party underground, which has always favoured their growth; for, like a weed, they flower in adversity.
My advice is to keep them out in the open. Let everyone see their leaders and their party members. By all means tell the people, retell the people, and tell the people again what the communists stand for, and make them campaign as you and I campaign, in the open market places of political ideas. The Canadian loves freedom for himself; but he detests and fears insecurity for his family; and if we deprive him of his present modest measure of security he will again, as he did in 1930 and in 1934, listen to those who propose that he trade in his freedom.
Poverty is the great catalyst that drives an exhausted society to communism. In Europe not only have they had poverty, but on top of that they have exploitation, corruption, race hatred, discrimination, inequality of opportunity and injustice. In this country, if we keep things healthy economically for the masses of the people, there is nothing at all that we need worry about. But if we permit collapse again we shall once more have some form of red peril, no matter under what name it travels.
The challenge is to make democracy work, for when democracy becomes positive communism becomes negative. As for myself, I have sufficient confidence in our institutions to believe that they will survive the onslaught of political controversy. They will grow and improve and benefit our people. Reason, history and experience tell me that this bill, if passed, will play into the hands of the communists, and that is the last thing I want to do.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I have a word of disagreement with the last speaker. If I have I shall have to read his speech carefully to find out what it is; because his sentiments were expressed as I should like to be able to express mine. However I am going to deal with the matter from a slightly different point of view, from the point of view of an ordinary everyday Canadian citizen who has a tremendous belief in the past of our country, a tremendous faith in the future of it, and an infinitely greater faith in the intelligence of the Canadian people to listen to, screen and accept or reject ideas that are submitted to them. If our eighty years of responsible government have not taught all of us that we as a people are capable of doing that, then we have not been able to learn the lessons of history.

Criminal Code Amendment
Furthermore, we have in the mother country some valuable lessons. They have never attempted a thing of this kind. I have been in London myself-and a great many other hon. members who have been overseas have been there-and listened to the variety of speeches one will hear in Hyde Park, in Albert Hall and in other places. Only the other day a man told me that he was over there during the war and attended an open air meeting being held around the smoking ruins where one of the big rocket bombs of the Germans had fallen. Right there a man was standing up making a speech, condemning the British government for its treatment of German prisoners of war, and nobody tried to take him down off his box; nobody interfered with him. They let him talk, I do not suppose he had the slightest effect on the government's treatment of prisoners of war. But when the people can believe in the right of free speech to the extent that they will allow a speech of that kind around the smoking ruins of one of their buildings where probably lives were lost, it indicates that they have learned the value of democracy, or, as the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll) sajrs, the open-market discussion of political ideas and other kinds.
I hold in my hand a little clipping from The Economist of London, and it is headed, "No United Kingdom 'Witch-Hunt'." It reads as follows:
Action against professing communists in the United Kingdom government service has long seemed desirable, but it must not be allowed to develop into the kind of excesses which have lately been witnessed in Washington. There may be something laughable in the spectacle of Hollywood reduced to a jelly of fear of "radicalism"; but there is something tragic in it, too. In the last resort, democracies must work out their own means of self-protection by their own democratic method. That is the only final assurance that it cannot happen here.
That is something that everybody can learn. We come back closer to home, and while I am not a supporter of my hon. friends opposite-[DOT] there was a time when I was, many years ago in my juvenile life when I had not seen the light-I retain the democratic right, Mr. Speaker, to go back there if I want to.
Mr. JOHNSTON; You would hate to do so.

subtopic: ORGANIZATIONS ADVOCATING OVERTHROW OP CONSTITUTED AUTHORITY
speechtext:
I am not going to do so, but I have the democratic right to do so, or to support my hon. friends here, or my hon. friends there, and I want nobody to take that right away from me. I will oppose any attempt to do that, and I equally oppose the attempt to prevent anybody else from expressing his ideas. I do that on idealistic democratic grounds. But I also want to say, as the hon. member for Spadina has said, that there is a very good practical reason why I do not want to see a bill of this kind passed in this house.
It so happened that I attended the first meeting called to organize the communist party in that part of the country in which I lived shortly after world war I. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that things were more or less upset politically. Ideas were undergoing certain changes. There was questioning going on, and obviously everybody was imbued with what he thought was a new idea and was endeavouring to express it.
I went to that meeting and listened carefully to the man who came to tell us the story of what we could do for this country if we formed a communist party. When the time came to sign up members I had to make up my mind, and I did. I did not find in that meeting, or in the program suggested, the place where my political faith could find a home, and so I left the meeting and have never attended one of that kind since. But I have watched them closely, and I believe that the decision to which I came at that time was the right one. They still have no place for me in their particular organization, nor have I any desire to be there.
On the other hand, in our political life in this country I must, on behalf of those who wish to support me, go out into the open market of political ideas and take on all comers who do not believe as I do, and I am perfectly willing to do so. If any member on the other side wishes to come to my constituency and promote his ideas I am prepared to stand on the same platform with him and oppose his ideas and advocate my own. The same goes for my hon. friends over there or in any other part of the house and the same goes for those who believe in the communist idea.
At no time, however, have I ever suggested, and I hope I shall never so far lose my faith in democratic methods as to suggest, that because someone over there or over here, or anywhere else, does not agree with me I must prevent that person from having the right to say what he wishes to say. Certainly I will never suggest that such a person be put in jail or be outlawed or shot or treated in any other way that some others might treat us.
I am not alone in that belief. Responsible members on the Liberal side apparently feel the same way, for I have a report that appeared in the newspapers, from the Canadian Press, wherein the Secretary of State
Criminal Code Amendment

(Mr. Gibson), who is not in his seat at the moment, is reported to have said at a meeting held at Kitchener-and these words are in quotation marks:
"Some people suggest that the communist party should be outlawed and its papers banned. I do not believe this is the answer . . . if we have nothing better to offer than the communists, then we have no excuse for opposing them; but if, as we generally believe, our system is superior, then our people of all groups and classes have a right to know in what ways they benefit by supporting our democratic system." *
There is a place where the Secretary of State and I can meet on common ground, and that is, I expect, rather rare for him and me.
I wish to point out also that a bill of this kind exhibits two characteristics, to neither of which I should like to see Canadians subject. It indicates either a lack of faith in the Canadian voter or else a childish fear of something because we have not the courage to get out and face it and take the necessary steps to make it impossible for the thing we fear to grow.
In another debate in this house the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka) put some figures on the record. His speech will be found at page 3555 of Hansard of May 3 of this year. He took his figures from the World Report of April, 1947. The figures were released in London, according to his statement, and he gave the size in numbers and percentage of population in various countries of the communist party. In Canada, his figures indicate, there are 23,000, or one-fifth of one per cent- [DOT]2 per cent.
I remember the early days of Hitler's regime when he was turning his hatred upon the people of the Jewish race and when he tried to make and finally succeeded in making the German people believe that the whole future of Germany was endangered by allowing this small section of the population to live. He made it stick so well that these people were almost eliminated.
At that time the Jewish population of greater Germany w'as, I believe, something less than one per cent of the total population. Do we want something like that to happen here? Do we wan t to debase ourselves so far as to try to bring about the conditions recommended by this bill, because we are afraid of one-fifth of one per cent of the population of Canada who have been active in this country for something like twenty-eight years?
I cannot conceive of an idea of that kind emanating from a Canadian citizen whose forebears pioneered this country and took an active part in the development of our democratic institutions, a Canadian who, like myself,

knows only this as his native land, who believes in our institutions, in the land where his particular racial group and mine have learned to get along together in amity without threats, except on the part of a few fools, to go and shoot each other. I cannot understand such a man bringing in a bill of this kind. It seems to me inconceivable.
If this bill had come from a newcomer to Canada who had emigrated from a country where they had never had the advantages of our historical background, I could understand it. But from a fellow Canadian like myself, I am frankly unable to understand how it could be proposed.
Let us see whether there is truth in the dangers that these people represent. We are told that one of their first points of attack is among the working-class organizations. Mr. Speaker, for a great number of years I have been very active in the farm organizations of Saskatchewan, big ones and little ones, from small institutions comprising a few people who handle in a co-operative way coal, wood, gasoline, and things of that kind, to the larger ones that handle the great grain marketing and the great distribution of all commodities.
We have communists in Saskatchewan. There may be some in the co-operative movement; in fact, I would be amazed if there were not. I expect that some have probably tried to gain official positions in the elective fields of these organizations, but of all the organizations I know, I am aware of only one co-operative farmers organization in Saskatchewan that has one communist on the board of directors, and he is there, not by any claim to political superiority by reason of his beliefs but because the people who elected him believe he is a competent director of the organization. If he attempted to introduce any of his ideas into the operation of that organization he would suffer defeat at the next election.
Of all those organizations, I know of not a single one that is to the slightest extent dominated, among its elected officers, by communists. I hold in my hand their News Letter, volume 3, No. 4, of April, put out by the Co-operative Union of Saskatchewan, and I wish to show how co-operatives believe in democratic performance, in democratic practices and in democratic activities in all their fields. I will say this, and it cannot be disputed, that no co-operative organization in this country that I have ever heard of has ever endeavoured to prevent, by law or repression, even the kind of private enterprise they are opposing, from continuing, although we have frequently had some types of private enterprise that have tried with some success to persuade the present government to make

it more difficult for co-operatives to grow than they have for some of the great semimonopolies in this country. Mr. Speaker, when the people of Canada learned about the budget they were very much disappointed, for many good reasons. I do not intend to speak very long in English; a little later I shall continue in French. I should like to draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that if social credit policies had been applied in this country we would not have had to face the things we are facing today. During the war, social credit policies were partly applied; for instance, the subsidies given to producers, which constituted a step toward the social credit policy of just prices. If this policy were still followed in this countiy we would not face shortages of mei-chandise and complaints from the consumers.
During the war we made gifts to other countries. In peacetime it would be no harder to make those gifts to our own people, and they would be completely satisfied. All during the war we never heard anything about a shortage of money in this country, though they say that in order to carry on the war we were obliged to tax the people heavily, that the people were paying all these expenses, and so on. When war was declared in 1939 the people of Canada were not able to finance it because we were just like a lot of broken nails. We had been starved for the ten previous years. However, just overnight in 1939 we were able to find the money with which to build up the strongest war machine we had ever had in this country. It should be just as easy to build up in peacetime a machine to assist our people.

May I quote the following excerpt from an article by Mr. Leopold Richer which I have read in the newspaper Notre Temps:
There remains as a bulwark against the rise of communism and socialism, the impressive fortress of American capitalism. However, in the neighbouring country as everywhere else, private enterprise is attacked from without and from within. From outside, by all those forces which lead, particularly in Europe, toward the state control of production and wealth sources. From within, by its own abuses, its static condition, its blindness, and, its slowness in adapting itself to new conditions.
Western Europe is being helped in her fight against communism; but is it known that victory is thus being ensured to socialism in Europe? Now after all what is socialism if not a bridge thrown across the abyss of bloody revolutions to enable people to cross over peaceably from capitalism to communism? Does one realize finally what a ridiculous situation the capitalist countries find themselves in? They are providing the enemy with arms.
Mr. Richer adds:
Even if it is understood that North America should go to the aid of starving and impoverished Europe, one can rest assured that this will not ensure the survival of private enterprise. Is the latter looking for an ideology? This ideology already exists. It is there, within the said enterprise and its social realm.
As Mr. Esdras Minville recently reminded the members of the Montreal Chamber of Commerce: "The world of tomorrow will either be Christian or communist. Business men cling to freedom of endeavour and to private enterprise. And rightly so, because these are important fundamentals of a social order based upon the respect of human dignity. But if business has rights, it also has duties to perform, the first of *which is to serve society."
If capitalism is to survive, it can pursue but one objective. It must aim at making private enterprise serve the community. But once this objective has been set, we get a new outlook on the future and private enterprise can save the community many tragic upheavals.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that no intelli-, gent citizen, having read that article, should1 be satisfied with saying: "How beautiful and logical". On the contrary, everyone should make up his mind to follow that lead in order that we may achieve the results which we are seeking.
The problem today lies more in the distribution of goods than in their production. Our

industries, both primary and secondary, could produce even more goods if they were only given an incentive to do so. What we are lacking is buying power in the hands of the consumers. The replacement of man-power by machine creates a problem to which there must be a better solution than ever-increasing unemployment.
Today, production depends more and more on mechanization. The worker, who has been replaced by the machine, is no longer remunerated. He loses his wages and everything. If we come to the point where machine replaces the worker, instead of serving him, man will be enslaved.
The purpose of economy is not to provide employment, but to satisfy the needs of man. Such is the purpose of economy. Those who do not think that it should serve the people are simply off the track.
Full employment is not an impossibility. For instance, instead of using fifty men or a steam shovel that takes the place of some two or three hundred men, we could bury the steam shovel and put some five or six hundred men to work with teaspoons. That would give work to everyone. It would be a way of achieving full employment as it is advocated by members of the C.C.F. and by our Liberal friends opposite.
By applying every social credit principle, the policy advocated by the Electors' Union would solve and cure the economic ills that are rife in Canada.
The Social Credit party suggests a cure that would save the people as well as free and private enterprise. Other groups, as I have just pointed out, offer full employment or similar plans that, in short, are just as effective as a poultice applied to a wooden leg.
In the budget speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) told us that he could not reduce the personal income tax; the people must understand, he said, that even with more money, they could not buy more than they do at present. There is at least one course they could take, but that is quite out of the question today. Indeed, &8 per cent of our workers earn less than S2,000 a year and they are burdened with debt practically the whole year round. If they had less taxes to pay they could afford to pay their bills. Many such people, hundreds of them, are in urgent need of money.

They have barely enough to live on, $2,000 to $2,500 a year and they would rather spend that money for their family, but they are prevented from doing so. It is alleged that they could not purchase more commodities with this money, but they could at least pay for what they are buying now.
The program of the Union of Electors is more than ever a practical one,, and those who do not now recognize it as such will have to admit it before long. If we must wait till we are shaken out of our complacency, it will not take long. It is no secret that the communists are gaining throughout the world. Once again, I say that we must do something at home.
When we ask that all revenues of less than $3,000 a year be tax-free, such a provision is possible and logical. No valid reasons can be given in this house for the maintenance of a tax on all incomes over and above $750 for single persons and $1,500 for married people, when we, as members of parliament, enjoy exemptions of $2,750 for single persons and $3,500 in the case of married people. We find it to be a good thing for ourselves; it is logical and none of us voices any criticism; we are glad to have that exemption but let us not forget that all constituents in our respective counties and every Canadian would also be delighted and pleased to be relieved in some measure from the burden of income tax.
And now, a word concerning the old age pensions of $60 per month at age 60. Some may ask, where will the money come from? Where did it come from during the war? Let us get it from the same source.
Tonight I shall discuss not the methods but the results that are desired. Let us ask ourselves whether Canada can produce enough to pay a $60 monthly pension without the means test, to people in the sixties.
Then we should grant monthly pensions of $60 to our incapacitated or disabled people after they reach the age of 21. No one could assert that Canada is unable to produce sufficient to ensure our incapacitated of disabled people a monthly pension of $60 at the age of 21, when we are in a position to grant pensions to our office workers after the age of 60. If we can give huge sums outside Canada we should certainly be able to give some assistance to those who need it in this country.
The fourth point is the monthly $20 national dividend which we demand. That dividend is
still possible. As I said at the outset, family allowances are based on the same principle as that dividend. Moreover, the latter would not be based on laziness as some claim; on the contrary it would be based on and linked with production, and production itself cannot materialize if it is not linked with work.
Dividends would be handed out for labour. The higher the level of production, the fatter these dividends would be. There is absolutely nothing illogical or unfeasible about it today in our country. In the present state of industries, equipment and mechanical devices, we must find a remedy to the social unrest that prevails among our people. In a letter to the King of Sardinia, the Monsignor Rendu, Bishop of Annecy, wrote as follows:
The progress of industry has given rise to such odious abuses that one has to go back to the times of paganism to find the same degree of callousness and contempt of humanity as exists today. What astonishes me most is that public opinion or what is generally called by that word does not rise against this ever-increasing disorder which engulfs the community like a wave blown by a storm from the middle of the ocean. The abolition of slavery was the source of a noble enthusiasm . . . ; however there is no one to suggest a remedy to this most painful and loathsome disease of humanity. The wailings of its victims are plainly heard, but no one dares raise his voice from fear of those who press them in an effort to extract gold from them.
The same conditions prevail today. Everyone is afraid to raise his voice against finance, against those who control money and credit or against those who are treating man as a piece of machinery. Under social credit from the social standpoint, we are not afraid of attacking evil wdiere it exists and of applying the remedy where it is needed instead of resorting to futile remedies.
If we do not want communism in Canada, let us at least provide honest means of livelihood to each and everyone of our citizens. Let there be among us the rich, the not-so-rich, millionaires and the poor, but we should see that in Canada nobody lacks the necessaries of life. Let us at least guarantee basic necessities.
In his encyclical Quadragesimo Anno, Pope Pius XI expresses himself as follows:
For then only will the economic and social organism be soundly established and attain its end when it secures for all and each those goods which the wealth and resources of nature, technical achievement, and the social organization

of economic affairs can give. These goods should be sufficient to supply all needs and an honest livelihood, and to uplift men to _ that higher level of prosperity and culture which, provided it be used with prudence, is not only no hindrance but is of singular help to virtue.
Mr. Speaker, I will fell my hon. friends from the other side of the house that if social credit is no good, if it is a dangerous thing, a thing to be feared, what is there to stop the government from applying in Canada the social doctrine of the church? Who prevents them from doing that? It is the financiers, the people who control money and credit,, who are only too glad to lean on us to make war, to make the gun-makers wealthy, but when it comes to making the Canadian population wealthy there is no more money. The money-makers are for war; they like war. Then they come and take away from us the money we have been able to make during or after the war, and that for many years to come.

For the last month there has been vile propaganda against that northern section- of the province of Quebec which I have the honour to represent in this house. It was even said that machine-guns had been found at Yal d'Or, in the cellar of the member for Pontiac. This whole story is a malicious fabrication, reflecting on the population of the northern part of the province. At Val d'Or as elsewhere, the people are peaceful, peace-loving, mindful of their own business. They are not communists. There are no more communists in Val d'Or or in Rouyn -than here in the house at Ottawa, or in Montreal. We have no such people. Those living in the north are for the most part Catholics. In my constituency they are Social Crediters, which means that they are anti-communists.

Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) should see his

way clear to satisfy the numerous demands that come from the city of Val d'Or, and provide it with a post office. We also ask for the establishment of a rural mail delivery service in all the parishes of the county of Pontiac, which are all agricultural or colonization parishes. Some people there have to walk as much as five or six miles to fetch their mail. We ask for a rural mail delivery service. We are entitled to it, but here again I suppose money will be lacking.
For two years now we have been demanding a home delivery mail service for the twin cities of Rouyn and Noranda. The Postmaster General (Mr. Bertrand) says that a post office should be constructed at Noranda or at Rouyn, and that he does not know what to do. Those people in the north want to be told, not where the post office is to be built, but whether they can have their mail delivered at the door. As far as the means employed are concerned, that is the government's business, the Post Office Department's business. The population wants results. If we get none there, because the member is not a Liberal, it means that it is just the same as in Russia where communist methods are employed. The representatives of the people must be respected, whether they be Liberals, Conservatives. C.C.F. or Social Crediters. When their constituency needs something, let them have it, instead of waiting till the next election to give them empty promises. Those are the things which my constituency most urgently needs. I hope that the responsible ministers will see to it that those requests are satisfied as soon as possible. The whole population suffers from injustice at present. We are entitled to these services and have a right to expect results.
In conclusion may I state that, from the economic point of view, social credit provides a solution. If it is not good, let another one be brought forward. Its philosophy is not a materialistic one. On the contrary it is a good spiritual philosophy and we will fight for its application throughout Canada.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my contribution to the debate will be brief, for I do not intend to indulge in any detailed criticism of the budget but merely to endorse what already has been very well said by other members of this party.
I find that the manner of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is so engaging that, as far as I am concerned, in his administering of a very bitter pill I am somewhat disarmed.

The Budget-Mr. Barrett
However, in spite of his assurance that the medicine will be good for us, I think the harshness and bad taste of the dose will not only nullify any good effects which theoretically it should have, but tend to destroy that confidence which is so necessary between patient and physician if a cure is to be effected.
The disease, the minister tells us, is inflation; the cure, high taxation. But this heavy burden of taxation, especially as it bears upon the lower income group, is having a definite effect in slowing up production; and increased production, it seems to me, which would help to satisfy the pent-up demand, would be a much better way of beating inflation than taking the people's money away from them so that they will be too hard up to buy what they want.
My conception of the function of government is probably an old-fashioned one, but I believe that government should interfere as little as possible with the ordinary affairs and the lives of the people. If injustices are being perpetrated by any one group, it is the duty of the government to correct and curb those abuses. But otherwise I think they should, as much as possible, leave the people alone to run their own affairs and they should make conditions such that the people will be encouraged to make a reasonable profit rather than discourage and discredit them for so doing.
I deplore this ever-growing tendency toward government interference in private business which is so greatly advocated by my hon. friends to the left and which is practised by my hon. friends opposite. I shall probably be dubbed as a Tory reactionary for taking this stand. Since that term is bandied about so often, I think it worthwhile to inquire into just who are the reactionaries in this house. According to my understanding, a reactionary is one who persists in advocating outworn and discredited policies. Socialism is nothing more than state management, state control and state paternalism. It is the oldest form of government known to society.
In the olden days of the tribal system it probably worked fairly well, in that stage of social development. The chief had full control over the lives of the people of his clan, and looked after them in a paternal way. As civilization advanced, this system developed into the old feudal system, and for a great many years that worked well, at that time. But society has outgrown that. It is now outworn and discredited. On the other hand, the system which this party stands for and supports, that of the greatest freedom of the individual-out of which have grown all the freedoms which we enjoy, such as the freedom of association, universal suffrage, freedom of elections and 5849-278
all the other benefits of democracy-is the most modern, the most advanced system, and has been more conducive to human happiness than any other system recorded by history. I therefore leave it to the judgment of the house as to who are the reactionaries.
Moreover, while our hon. friends of the C.C.F. are extremely voluble in repudiating these embarrassing advances which are being made to them by communism-and I quite acknowledge their sincerity in this repudiation -I must point out to them that, while their methods of approach and their methods of administration differ vastly from those of communism, in the long run the ultimate aim is the same, namely state control of the people. In fact, as Lord Lothian said a few years ago at an Empire club banquet, communism is the only form of socialism that will work. In this connection, with your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read into the record a resolution which I have received from a group of Ukrainian citizens in my own constituency. It is as follows:
We, Canadians of Ukrainian origin, numbering 80 gathered ait a public meeting in Waterford, Ontario, May 16, 1948, unanimously resolved to bring to your attention the following:
1.	In 1918, by the will of forty million Ukrainian people on their ethnographic lands of Europe, a democratic Ukrainian national republic was formed, which was recognized by the western powers.
2.	The Ukrainian national republic was annihilated by the armed aggression of the Muscovite Bolsheviks between the years 1918 and 1920, and a fictitious totalitarian state the so-called Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic was formed, which, even today exists due to the dictatorship of the ruling communist party and to the terrorism of the secret political police.
3.	Since that time the Ukrainian people have struggled unceasingly against the Soviet occupants, viz.: millions of lives lost in that struggle, the present uprising of the Ukrainian partisan army, and the new 300,000 Ukrainian political refugees in the allied occupation zones of Germany.
4.	Only after occupying the Ukraine, and annihilating the more intelligent and more active elements of the Ukrainian people by mass executions, by banishments, and by artificial famine, were the Muscovite communists able to commence the realization, of their imperialistic plans for undermining the whole world.
5.	The Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, with its anti-national, totalitarian, terrorist regime, appears as the greatest threat to world peace, world freedom, culture and the Christian religion.
6.	By means of revolutions, civil wars, economic crises and subversive acts of its fifth column communist parties in every country, the U.S.S.R. aims to overthrow the existing democratic regimes and to form vassal states, based on the dictatorship of communist minority.
7.	The communist parties of the world, under various aliases, are in reality branches of Moscow's communist party of Russia and a fifth column of the U.S.S.R., whose orders guide their
The Budget-Mr. Knowles

activities. Their activity is aimed at the destruction and overthrow of countries wherein they function.
Therefore, we appeal to the Canadian government and especially to its united nations representatives:
1.	To investigate, to introduce and to support at the united nations forum, the just requests of the forty million Ukrainians in regard to the renewal of the Ukrainian democratic national republic on their ethnographic territories.
2.	To question the right of Mr. D. Manuilski, who has been appointed by and represents the occupational Eussian regime, the right to speak in the name of the Ukrainian people.
3.	To point out to the members of the united nations the threat to world peace of the present totalitarian U.S.S.R. government with its antinational regime and its imperialistic foreign policy.
4.	To outlaw the so-called Labour Progressive party, which is a branch of the Russian communist party and a fifth column of U.S.S.R. The L.P.P. is not a Canadian party because its headquarters are outside Canada and this party's activity is aimed at exterminating the democratic regime in Canada.
5.	To extend a sanctuary on Canadian soil to the Ukrainian political refugees, who at present are found in western Germany and Austria. These peoples are anti-communists, and are representatives of every walk of life. During the last three years under the protection of the western allies they have displayed their skill in organizational and constructive work.
These displaced persons if assisted to settle in Canada would spearhead the movement and combat communism since they are victims of its menace. We feel that the settling of these people in Canada will raise the standard of Canada culturally and economically. In the present grave international crisis these people look with foreboding at the future and have no opportunity for a total expression of their constructive abilities.
We trust that you, being acquainted with the foregoing, will draw the necessary and fair conclusions and meet our request with approval. We remain,
Faithfully yours,
Mike Podolak, Chairman of meeting.
John Danyeevich,
Secretary.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his budget speech the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said we should view the national budget in relation to the whole economy of the country. He went further and said we should think of it in terms not only of the present but also of the future.
With that sentiment I thoroughly agree, but I fail to find in the budget speech or in the policies of the government any implementation of that high principle. As far as the budget itself is concerned, it seemed to me that the Minister of Finance applied that principle of planning our national affairs in relation to our whole economy only with respect to the

national debt. To him it seemed a matter of supreme concern that we plan everything to make as large a reduction as possible in our national debt. All of us feel a measure of sympathy with that idea, for it is in keeping with something most of us go through personally. We find that debt is a millstone around one's neck, and that it is highly desirable to get rid of it if at all possible. But it is also true in the experience of ordinary human beings that most people like to live for something else than just paying off debt. Most people like to enjoy life in the process, and to feel that they have something to look forward to. I suggest that there is a parallel between that ordinary human experience and the problem which faces us in planning our national economy. I believe it is our job as a parliament, and the job of the government, to find a balance between reducing the debt as far as that can be done, and at the same time making provision for improving the standard of living and providing our Canadian people with an opportunity to enjoy life here and now.
Just in passing, I should like to remind the minister and the house that if his position were completely logical it would mean that we should do our best to get the national debt down to some small figure, such as it was a number of years ago. When we look at some of the statistics with which we have been furnished we find that in 1933 our national debt was only about 82,500 million. In 1947. on the other hand, our national debt was over $13,000 million. Most of us have memories of 1933 which are much more bitter than those of 1947. The fact is that in the year of the infinitely smaller national debt we had the worst depression this country has ever known, but in the year of the huge national debt to which I have referred we had what the government, at least, calls a time of high prosperity. I do not say one is the cause of the other, but certainly these figures disprove the suggestion that by simply reducing our national debt to some smaller figure we would bring back prosperity. What counts is not the size of the national debt but the level of our economic activity, and the production of the goods and services that go to make up the standard of living of our people.
As a matter of fact, this point was driven home to the house a good many times during the course of the war by the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) when he was Minister of Finance. Time and again he was chided by Mr. Hanson, then leader of the official opposition, over the huge debt which was being piled up. The minister found this chiding somewhat to his liking, for it enabled him to reply that this huge national debt was but an

The Budget-Mr. Knowles
index of the increased productivity of the country. Many times he told us he had no fear of our ability to carry a much larger national debt as long as we had a high level of economic activity and high productivity. So I suggest that the aim of the government's budgetary proposals and the aim of parliament should be not simply the reduction of the national debt to some hypothetically low figure, but rather the raising of the level of production and the standard of living of the Canadian people.
I felt that the best part of the budget speech was the part the minister did not read. As a matter of fact, I want to compliment the minister and his officials on the way in which the white paper was put together this year. In his speech the minister indicated that there were certain new departures; and I have found it extremely interesting and valuable to look through the statistics contained in the budget white paper. I am sure these figures will be very useful to us in time to come. I was particularly pleased with the way in which the minister had prepared for us not only figures relating to government accounts but figures relating to our national economy in the broader sense. I am interested also in the figures he gave relating to the amount of money spent by governments at all three levels in relation to the total national income of the country as a whole.
Some hon. members may fear that having said this, I shall be launching into a reading of a lot of these figures. That is not my intention tonight. I do wish to call attention, however, to the figures in the appendix to the budget, on page 4111 of Hansard, where a table appears headed, "Personal disposable income per capita". This table, like many others in this appendix, gives comparisons for the years 1939, 1944, 1946 and 1947. The particular table to which I refer indicates quite clearly that there has been a considerable increase in the amount of personal disposable income per capita in this country since 1939, and I happen to know that the figure in 1939 was considerably higher than it was in 1933. Even with the increases that have taken place, however, we find that the average personal income per capita in Canada! for 1947, before the deduction of taxes, was $804. The direct personal tax amounted on an average to $63, which left a net personal disposable income of $741 for every man, woman and child in this country.
It all depends on one's approach to this subject whether that is a good figure or not. When one thinks of it in terms of average individual income it does not sound very much, but when someone points out that it is the 5849-278i
average income that people can spend for all the goods and services they need to keep alive, the average income of every man, woman and child, then it might be said that it is pretty fair. For example, if the average for every man, woman and child is close to $750, to use round figures, it would mean that a family of four-a man, his wife and two children- would have an average annual spendable income of $3,000. Again I say that sounds very good when one speaks in terms of averages.
But nothing is more deceptive in statistics than averages and that rule certainly holds good in this case. It so happened that about a day or two after we got the budget and this interesting appendix which the minister gave us with it, his colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann), presented us with a green book entitled, "Taxation Statistics." This book bears the publication date of September, 1947. Again I am grateful to a department of government for what it has done in compiling useful statistics. I wish to refer to some figures found on pages 116 and 117 of this new and interesting book. The figures on these pages are headed as follows:
Estimated distribution of taxpayers, income, and revenue by income class and by marital status and dependents.
These figures are for the taxation year 1946, which is the last year for which these statistics are available, and one can understand that they could not be any later than that just yet. I wish to make a comparison between the average personal disposable income which the Minister of Finance gave in the appendix to the budget with the figures furnished by the Minister of National Revenue. I do not want anyone to say I am dealing with figures that are not comparable, so in the table given by the Minister of Finance on page 7 of the appendix I shall take the figure for 1946 and compare it with those given by the Minister of National Revenue for the same year. In that year the average personal income in Canada was $769 before taxes were deducted. With the deduction of taxes, it is brought/ down to $704. It is a question which of those' figures one should take for the purpose I have in mind, but I suggest that the round figure of $750 is fair enough, and for my purposes it is on the conservative side.
What I am anxious to do is to show hon. members how deceptive that average is. It is very nice to say that every man, woman and child has $750 a year to spend on the things he needs. Thus it might be said that $3,000 a year for a family of four is not too bad. But what is the picture as given to us
The Budget-Mr. Knowles

by the Minister of National Revenue in his book, "Taxation Statistics"? To begin with, I may say there are several columns in these pages headed "single no dependents", "single one dependent", "single two or more dependents", "married no dependent", "married one dependent", "married two dependents", "married three dependents", and so on. I intend to take the figures from only three columns. The three I have chosen are "married one dependent", "married two dependents" and "married three dependents". In ot,her words, these are families of three, four and five persons. I have taken them as being a sort of average Canadian family.
If it were true that the Canadian people have this glorious average of $750 a year per person it would mean that families of three should have an income of $2,250 a year. But what is the story for a family of three persons, namely, a married couple with one dependent? There were in the year I am considering, 1946, 423,520 taxpayers in that class. Of those 423,520 taxpayers in the class of families of three, only 161,020 had $2,250 or more. On the other hand, 262,500 of them had incomes of less than $2,250, or, in other words, less than this glorious Canadian average.
Let me put it in percentages. Only 38 per cent of families of three persons who pay taxes had the average income or better; 62 per cent of them had less than the average. Bear in mind this further fact that I am taking only the figures for those in the taxation bracket. If you add to the 62 per cent to which I have just referred the families of three that do not pay income tax that are below the exemption levels, the number of which is not given, you raise to a much higher figure those families of three Canadians who are below the average to which I have referred.
Let me go into the next column which deals with married persons with two dependents, or, in other words, a family of four. If the glorious Canadian average meant anything it would mean that a family of four should have an income of four times $750, or $3,000 of disposable personal income. But what is the story of families of four? According to the figures furnished by the Minister of National Revenue, there were 294,616 taxpayers in the class of families of four, or married with two dependents. Of those 294,616, only 48,166, or 17 per cent, had the average or better. On the other hand, 246,450, or 83 per cent, had incomes in 1946 below the glorious average.
Again I point out that that figure of 246,450 families of four persons having less than the average income takes into account only those who paid taxes. If you add to that figure the families of four that had incomes so small that

they did not pay taxes at all and therefore are not included in the taxation statistics, the percentage of Canadian families of four having less than the average would be even higher than 83 per cent.
I move over into the next column which is headed "married three dependents", or in other words, families of five. What is the story there? Again, if the average of $750 meant anything it should mean that families of five have an income of $3,750 a year. I find in the case of these families of five, in 1946 there were 142,524 who paid taxes, and of that number only 14,224-

speechtext: Where did you get that figure of 14,224?

speechtext:
That is the best promise we ever got from the ministerial benches. I want to make one further comment about this class, namely, families of five. I have taken as the average $3,750, namely, five times the

The Budget-Mr. Knowles
average individual income of $750, and I have shown that 90 per cent of the families of five have less than that average. Actually in the group "married three dependents", namely, families of five, there are 56,800 who have less than half the average, and that figure of 56,800 represents 40 per cent of the married taxpayers in this country who have three dependents.
I point out again that my figures are on the conservative side, because they do not include the thousands of persons that there are in each of these categories whose incomes are below the exemption levels altogether.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that this turns that glorious Canadian average of $750 per person into a pretty sorry picture when one has to face the fact that there are that many Canadian families trying to get along on incomes so far below the average. This average income is very nice if you have it or if you are in the brackets above it, but it is poor solace and poor comfort to those who are away down below to be told that, on the whole, things are so glorious in this country.
There are two comments I want to make on the statistics to which I have just referred. The first is. if I may go along with the line of thought that was in the mind of the Minister of National Revenue, that these figures support the criticism that has been made from many quarters of this house against the Minister of Finance for his failure to increase the tax exemption levels. Others have pointed out, and I will not take time to repeat it, what has happened to the cost of living. The Minister of Finance himself pointed that out very effectively in his speech when he told us that it was the thing that had chiefly concerned all of us during the past year or so. What 1 am pointing out now is that it is no theoretical or hypothetical consideration but a real problem for thousands of Canadians whose total personal disposable income is so far below the Canadian average.
The other comment I make on the basis of these figures is that they reveal pretty poor planning on the part of the government of the day as far as the standard of living of our Canadian people is concerned, and it points up the need for tremendous improvements in our economic conditions both in terms of economic productivity and in terms of social security. I do not wish to go into these matters at any great length tonight, but I want to say a word or two in particular with regard to the second of the things I have just mentioned, namely social security.
If any government accepts it as its duty to make its budget have some beneficial effect
upon the life of the country; if, as the Minister of Finance said in his budget speech at page 4072 of Hansard-
In the world of today we must be prepared to undertake much that is new, much that is daring, much that is big.
-one of the places to start is in the field of social security, a need that is high-lighted by the kind of figures that I have given the house tonight taken from the government's own statistics. With so many of our people down in those income brackets where living is so tough, it is not good enough to plan for better programs of social security years or decades in the future-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The only people who are talking that way are the hon. member and other politicians who are doing it for political reasons. On economic grounds it is not sensible.
