subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it true that the Saskatchewan government has cut down the old age pension recently?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No; raised it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Saskatchewan old age pension is the basic $30 a month that is provided for by federal statute, plus a $5 supplement added by the Saskatchewan provincial government.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: And they all get it.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Alberta pays a supplement; British Columbia pays a supplement, and there is a certain kind of supplement in Ontario.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A $10 supplement.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: With an additional means test. I am just stating these figures to give the total picture. Do not get me off into that, because it would be quite a long story. I frankly do not like the way in which we have been led into making old age pensions a political football and tossing it back and forth from the federal government to the provinces, or from one province to another. In my view what should have been done is something along the line which was proposed in the government's proposals to the provinces back in 1945.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As a matter of fact, your government did cut it.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They never did any such thing.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I happen to come from Manitoba; therefore it is not my government. But Saskatchewan at no time reduced the pensions payable to the old age pensioners in the province.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They withdrew the $5 supplement last fall.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The story of the Saskatchewan old age pensions was this: first $20 years ago, then raised to $25 in 1943 when this government did it here, raised to $28 a few years later by the Saskatchewan government itself, then raised to $30 a month about two years ago, and raised to $35 a month a few months ago. At no time has it been reduced.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is it not a fact that last fall when the Old Age Pensions Act amendment became effective the $5 supplement payment that Saskatchewan normally paid was withdrawn by the provincial government and restored at the beginning of the present year?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The $5 provincial grant that the province gave for about a year before this government came through with it was paid in lieu of the $5 which it was expected this government would provide. When they came through-

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada

speechtext: Pretty weak!

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: When it came through they did exactly what Premier Garson did in Manitoba, and nobody in this house had a word to say about that.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What was the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) complaining about out in Saskatchewan last October?

Saskatchewan was the only

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Minister of National Health and Welfare knows he is just indulging in the kind of practice that a certain magazine did. He is just carrying on this attempt to set the dominion against the provinces, and one province against another, and the old age pensioners suffer as a result of it.
I want to point out that the government of Saskatchewan has recently added another $5 and made it clear that it is paying what it regards as 25 per cent of a $50 a month pension, and it calls upon this government to give their share of the $50 a month pension.
Back in 1945, and I presume they meant it, the federal government made offers to the provinces, which included the expectation that this government would pay out $217 million for old age pensions in 1948. I know all the arguments about these two provinces down here who will not sit down and talk things over and agree upon something for the good of Canada as a whole, but this government apparently expected to spend $217 million on old age pensions in 1948. In this year's estimates the amount allotted is $65,000,000. I do not call that a good budget. With a surplus of $670 million, the government allow only $65,000,000 for old age pensions in the year 1948, when in 1945 they talked of putting aside $217 million for old age pensions.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. I must inform the hon. member that his time has expired.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext:
Just two minutes more, Mr. Speaker.
I was one of those who applauded mpst enthusiastically-I meant it and still do-when the Prime Minister made the announcement a few days ago in regard to health measures. We welcome a beginning in that field with all the enthusiasm we possess. But I cannot help noticing on the other hand that, whereas in 1945 there were proposals that involved the federal government spending $150 million per annum on health measures, we now have proposals laid 'before us for only $30,000,000. That kind of budgeting is not good enough for a government whose job it is to exercise some responsibility in respect of the well-being of the Canadian people as a whole. Our people have a right to expect something a great deal better.
There was more that I should like to have said, Mr. Speaker, but I will not trespass upon the time of the house. I thank you for the two minutes extra you have given me.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my first words will be to congratulate the treasurer, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) on the angelic patience he has shown all through this debate.

-over and over again to the same criticisms and requests. After having heard members criticize his failure to reduce the income tax, he will listen in a few days to a possibly greater number of members who, after all their criticisms, will ask him for increases, pensions of all kinds. They will tell him-like I am going to do tonight-that he should provide for public works, the construction of post offices, repairs to piers, et cetera. That is why I think he deserves to be congratulated, although those are the only congratulations I shall address to him tonight, for I believe, like Samuel Johnson, that praise like gold and diamonds owes its value to its scarcity. I ask him to continue, not always to pay attention to minor details but. as he has done, to face the future squarely without any fear of criticism, shaping his course with the knowledge that each of his actions and motions, as well as each of the words he has uttered are in the best interests of the people.
I heard last night the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher) tell us in perfect French, for which I congratulate him, that there are fundamental differences between his group and the communist party in so far as their respective ideologies, objects and methods are concerned. As regards the objects and methods, I might admit that often enough the hon. member is right. But in connection with any fundamental difference in ideology, I cannot see how the advocates of socialism, under whatever form, can know so little about it as to believe that they diverge from a theory which they have upheld from the very beginning, that is the Marxist theory. They are opposed to dictatorial methods used by communism, but let us remember that socialism and any form of government control of industries is a totalitarian method and if they do not propose to overthrow governments by force, if they plan to achieve that end through the popular vote, it is certainly not by advocating what can be called real democracy, because after all we must remember that in

Fortunately, the United Kingdom medical association stood firmly and the government had to fall back and let the people obtain medical care as it should be given, that is on the basis of devotion and self-sacrifice.

Mr. Speaker, I read in the Ottawa Journal today an article which is exactly along my line of thinking. In a certain debate, I referred to the position of Spain with respect to the united nations and especially the United States and the British commonwealth. As we are trading with Spain, I think I will be allowed to say a word about this article and even add to it. The Ottawa Journal said-and I am giving a hasty translation-that during the civil war in Spain, men who hold eminent positions in the communist party today were then acquiring their basic experience trying out, as de La Fontaine puts it in one of his fables, their first set of teeth. There we find Georgi Dimitrov who drew up plans for the international brigades in Spain and is now the Red dictator of Bulgaria. Tito was then known under the name of Joseph Brozovitch. He was in the forefront with Dimitrov and he is today the dictator of Yugoslavia. Klement Gottwald was a political commissar in Spain and today he is the strong man in Czechoslovakia. Andre Marty who was in active charge of the Dimitrov plan, is today a communist leader in France. I would say that he is the chief communist agent in France because he held a key position in the leadership of the communist party in that country. I am adding this to the article because the latter does not state that Andre Marty, his ancestor, was the communist leader in 1871, when Napoleon III fell. Luigi Longo, notwithstanding some newspaper items, holds in Italy a position exactly similar to that of Andre Marty in France. Longo presides over the military and political organization of the communist party in Italy. Mention is mostly made of Togliatti, but the real leader is Luigi Longo. These two men were making a first test of strength with Doctor Negrin the then president of the so-called democratic government of Spain. Therefore, those were the men who ran everything their own way in Spain and who were defeated by Franco.
Spain is accused today of being ruled by a fascist government and of still putting up with such a regime. At the same time, I am sorry *[DOT]849-279
to say, the united nations do not hold it against Russia to be party to two treaties, the first with the united nations, the second in relation to the three powers agreement of Japan, Germany and Italy. It is this secret document which was made public by the state department of the United States and which truly existed though its existence was denied, as it was bound to be, by Soviet Russia. In the case of Spain, with which we have commercial dealings, it is a crime, but no such crime attaches to Russia for having had double dealings with the countries of the world.
As I cannot speak indefinitely on Spain without being called to order-I thank Your Honour for your indulgence-I shall only put on record this question asked by the honourable member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion): What are the figures relative to our trade with Spain from 1936 to 1947?
We find that in 1936, our imports from Spain totalled $1,129,315 while our exports amounted only to $469,160, more briefly, in 1947, we bought $3,003,000 worth of goods from Spain but sent her commodities valued only at $940,594. To borrow a well-known saying from one of the high officials of the Department of External Affairs, this means that if the word "consul" is as old as trade, we should appoint a consul to Spain since we have been trading with that country for quite some time.
I understand that Mr. Glass who is in Lisbon with Mr. Morin is doing very creditable work, but, even if Franco is still leader of the Spanish government, we ought to appoint a consul who would supervise Canadian business in that part of the Iberian peninsula.
I said that my words of praise for the treasurer would be brief but I added that, like other honourable members, I would make various requests. I take the liberty of putting two on record. Since 1939 I have been pleading for the building of a post office at Donna-cona, one of the most prosperous new towns of the whole province of Quebec.
